Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/comparison.md

# How do the components compare with openpi's remote inference and LeRobot's?

It does not replace either one. openpi and LeRobot each ship a complete way to run a policy on a remote GPU: a server
that loads the model, and a client on the robot that talks to it. The components here load no model. The network layer is a set
of components for the connection underneath, and you use it in one of three ways:

| You run | You keep | You add from `sequence_ai.network` |
|---|---|---|
| openpi | openpi's server and client, unchanged | on the robot, `openpi.keep(policy)`, and `image_tools` from `sequence_ai.network.openpi` for pictures as JPEG; on the GPU, its server started through `python -m sequence_ai.network.openpi` |
| LeRobot's remote inference | LeRobot's server and client, unchanged | one Zenoh setting, in a file: `lerobot.keep_alive_file(path)` |
| your own server | your model and your handler | `connect()` on the robot; `one_write`, `ping`, `compressed`, `tcp_link` on the server |

This page compares what each one does and does not do, from source inspection: openpi at commit `215abfb`
(2026-08-24), LeRobot 0.7.0, and this package's components. Results from tests are marked as such. No head-to-head measurement
against openpi or LeRobot has been made.

## Side by side

| | openpi | LeRobot 0.7.0 | These components |
|---|---|---|---|
| What it is | A policy server and a client for openpi's models | A policy server and a remote executor for LeRobot's policies | Components for the connection; no model loading |
| Starts with | `uv run scripts/serve_policy.py --env=...` and `WebsocketClientPolicy(host, port)` | `lerobot-policy-server` and `lerobot-rollout --inference.type=remote` | `connect(url)` against your own server |
| Transport | WebSocket; the client opens one connection and reuses it | Zenoh, over TCP by default (`tcp/127.0.0.1:7447`) | HTTP on one persistent connection; options for WebSocket servers |
| Message format | msgpack, numpy arrays as raw bytes | msgpack, arrays as raw bytes | msgpack, numpy arrays as raw bytes; reads openpi's array layout and msgpack-numpy's |
| Camera frames | Resized on the robot with `image_tools.resize_with_pad` | Sent raw, or as JPEG (`encoding`, `jpeg_quality`) | `frames.resize_image` (its `"pad"` is openpi's `resize_with_pad`), `frames.encode` for JPEG and `frames.decode` on the server, `openpi.image_tools` and `openpi.patch()` for openpi's own client and server, lossless `compress` |
| Action chunks | `ActionChunkBroker` executes a chunk open-loop and requests the next when it is exhausted | Requests ahead of time, based on the turnaround it measured; aligns the new chunk with the one being executed; real-time chunking modes | None: `link.act()` returns your server's response |
| Robots on one server | Each connection's handler calls `policy.infer` itself; no batching across connections | One robot session; a second receives `busy` | Whatever your server does; `sequence_ai.engine` has `batcher`, `slack` and `replicas` |
| Timing it reports | `server_timing` in each response: the model's time in milliseconds | The turnaround of recent requests, kept by the client | p50, p95 and p99 of each request (`link.stats()`); each client's RTT and retransmissions, from the server's kernel (`tcp_link`) |

## The connection between requests

This is the one area where the network layer adds to both, so it is described in full.

| | openpi | LeRobot 0.7.0 | These components |
|---|---|---|---|
| What is sent on an idle connection | The `websockets` library's own ping, every 20 seconds by default: neither openpi's `serve(...)` call nor its client's `connect(...)` passes another interval | Zenoh's keep-alive frames: on an idle link between two peers, one every 1.5 s or less often (seen with Zenoh 1.10.2) | A ping every 100 ms while idle: from the robot (`connect()`, `window.Warm`, `openpi.keep`) or from a WebSocket server (`ping`); for Zenoh, a setting that makes it a frame every 100 ms |
| Congestion control on the robot's socket | Not set, so the machine's default | Not set by LeRobot; Zenoh opens the sockets | BBR where Linux allows it (`window.socket_options()`, `window.keep(sock)`); not for Zenoh, which opens its own sockets |
| TCP keepalive | Not set by openpi's client, nor by the `websockets` library under it | Not checked | Set, where the machine accepts the options |
| Tells you what the machine does | No | No | `window.check()`: whether the kernel restarts a window after a pause; `wifi_power.check()`: Wi-Fi power saving |

Why the interval matters: on Linux, a connection that has sent nothing for longer than its retransmission timeout (at
least its round-trip time (RTT) plus 200 ms) has its congestion window restarted. A ping every 20 seconds, or a frame
every 1.5 seconds, is longer than that, so neither keeps a window through a robot's sub-second pauses. That is a
statement about the mechanism. Whether it costs anything depends on the link, and on some links it cost nothing:
[Why does my robot's upload get slow after a pause?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/why-does-my-robots-upload-get-slow-after-a-pause.md)

## Test coverage

| | Tested | Not tested |
|---|---|---|
| openpi | `openpi.keep()` on openpi-client 0.1.2's real `WebsocketClientPolicy`, against a stand-in server speaking openpi's protocol on one machine ([`examples/quickstart_openpi.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/quickstart_openpi.py), `tests/network/test_openpi.py`). On a real link: `openpi.keep()`, and a server that pings, on a WebSocket connection of the kind openpi holds, with a stand-in for its client ([Measurements](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md)). For the technical report: openpi's policy server (commit `215abfb`, `pi05_droid`, on an L4) and its own client in a closed loop over a home connection, with no network component of this package on the connection; and the same server and client with `openpi.keep()`, from a Linux virtual machine on a home connection ([the table](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md#openpikeep-with-openpis-own-server-and-client)); and the same server pinging and decoding the pictures as `openpi.patch()` makes it, with the client sending them as JPEG as `openpi.image_tools` does, from a Mac on a home connection ([the table](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md#pictures-as-jpeg-with-openpis-own-server-and-client)). `openpi.patch()`, the command and `image_tools` against a server module built as openpi's (`tests/network/test_openpi_server.py`) | The server's pings and the JPEG apart; either, and `openpi.keep()`, with openpi's own server on more than one link |
| LeRobot | The keep-alive file on Zenoh 1.10.2: two idle peers on one machine then sent a frame about every 100 ms each way (`tests/network/test_lerobot.py`). On a real link: two Zenoh peers, with and without the file ([Measurements](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md)) | LeRobot's client or server, with or without the file |
| The components alone | Every measurement in the [README's table](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/README.md#results), with the tool in [`bench/`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/tree/main/bench) or the servers named there | Those measurements with openpi or LeRobot as the server |

## Which should I use?

- **You serve an openpi model (π0, π0-FAST, π0.5).** Use openpi's server and client. Start the server through
  `python -m sequence_ai.network.openpi` and import `image_tools` from it on the robot to send the pictures as JPEG, and
  add `openpi.keep(policy)` if the robot is on Linux and pauses between chunks:
  [How do I run π0 (openpi) on a remote GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-run-pi0-openpi-on-a-remote-gpu.md)
- **You serve a LeRobot policy.** Use LeRobot's remote inference. Add the Zenoh file on both sides:
  [How do I reduce the latency of LeRobot remote inference?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-reduce-the-latency-of-lerobot-remote-inference.md)
- **You have a model and no server yet, or your own server.** The network components are the transport:
  [How do I serve a robot policy from my own GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-serve-a-robot-policy-from-my-own-gpu.md) You then write, or
  take from another project, what openpi and LeRobot give you ready made: chunk playback on the robot, and the model's
  own input and output transforms.
- **Whichever you use,** [measure the link](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-measure-the-link-between-my-robot-and-my-gpu.md) first. The tool
  needs neither project.

## Where each fact was read

openpi, commit `215abfb217dbac7d5f1273282331b9b1866c0479` (Apache-2.0):

- `src/openpi/serving/websocket_policy_server.py`: the `serve(...)` call and its arguments; the handler that unpacks
  an observation, calls `self._policy.infer(obs)` and sends the response with `server_timing`.
- `packages/openpi-client/src/openpi_client/websocket_client_policy.py`: the client's `connect(...)` call and its
  arguments; `infer`.
- `packages/openpi-client/src/openpi_client/action_chunk_broker.py`: `ActionChunkBroker`.
- `packages/openpi-client/src/openpi_client/msgpack_numpy.py`: the array layout.
- `packages/openpi-client/src/openpi_client/image_tools.py`: `resize_with_pad`.
- `docs/remote_inference.md`: the two commands and the client-side resize.

LeRobot 0.7.0 (Apache-2.0):

- `lerobot/inference/factory.py`, `RemoteInferenceConfig`: `endpoint`, `refill_seconds`, `chunk_merge`, `encoding`,
  `jpeg_quality`, `zenoh_config_path`.
- `lerobot/inference/execution.py`: the turnaround kept from recent requests and the refill threshold made from it.
- `lerobot/remote_inference/server.py` and `lerobot/scripts/lerobot_policy_server.py`: one robot session for a server.
- `lerobot/transport/zenoh.py`, `ZenohConfig`: `config_file`, and the keys `build()` sets over it.
- `lerobot/transport/protocol/codec.py`: msgpack, arrays as raw bytes, JPEG.
- `lerobot/scripts/lerobot_rollout.py`: `--inference.type=remote`.

The `websockets` library, version 17.4: `ping_interval: float | None = 20` in the signatures of its `serve` and
`connect`.

If a fact here is out of date or wrong, please open an issue at
<https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/issues>.

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/components.md

# What does each network component do?

Each component is one file that you can use independently. This page gives, for each: the lines to add, why it
exists, what was measured and on which link, and the output of its example. The examples were run on a Mac with
Python 3.12, so the components that read the Linux kernel return `None` or `False` there.

| Client side | Server side | Both sides | Combined |
|---|---|---|---|
| [`window`](#window-the-congestion-window-kept-through-the-pauses) | [`ping`](#ping-a-server-side-ping) | [`msgpack_io`](#msgpack_io) | [`connect`](#connect-the-client-side-components-combined) |
| [`compress`](#compress-only-where-it-saves-time) | [`one_write`](#one_write-a-response-in-one-write) | [`latency_stats`](#latency_stats) | [`openpi`](#openpi-and-lerobot) |
| [`frames`](#frames-a-frame-resized-before-upload-and-decoded-on-the-server) | [`tcp_link`](#tcp_link-each-clients-link-read-from-the-kernel) | | [`lerobot`](#openpi-and-lerobot) |
| [`wifi_power`](#wifi_power-wi-fi-power-saving-detected) | [`compressed`](#compressed-decompress-what-the-client-compressed) | | [`bench/`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-measure-the-link-between-my-robot-and-my-gpu.md) |

What a component saves depends on your link, and every number below is given with the link it was measured on. The
inference components (`sequence_ai.engine`) are described in the [README](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/README.md#inference-layer).

## Client side

### `window`: the congestion window, kept through the pauses

```python
from sequence_ai.network import window

transport = httpx.HTTPTransport(socket_options=window.socket_options())    # BBR and TCP keepalive, where it can
window.keep(sock)                                                          # or BBR on your own socket

warm = window.Warm(ping=lambda: client.get("/ping"))    # a ping while the connection is idle
warm.used()                                              # each time you send on it

window.check()                                           # warns once: what this machine does after a pause
```

**Why.** On Linux a connection that sends nothing for longer than its retransmission timeout has its congestion window
restarted, so the next upload takes one extra round trip. A robot that sends a request every half second incurs it on
every request.

**Measured.**

- **BBR.** A robot sending a request every 0.53 s with 24 KB of frames, on a round-trip time (RTT) of about 21 ms: 40 of
  40 requests took one more round trip without it (21.5 ms), and none with it (0.5 to 3.0 ms).
- **Where the pause cost nothing.** On RTTs of about 101 and 241 ms the same robot took no extra round trip
  with the default settings (0 or 1 of 40 requests), until the link lost packets (38 to 40 of 40 at 1% loss) or the size
  of the request varied.
- **A ping while idle.** On an RTT of 226 ms, 162 KB uploads 3 s apart took 303.6 ms to arrive without the
  pings, and under 1 ms with them.

A ping cannot keep a window that the pings do not fill; BBR, or `tcp_slow_start_after_idle=0`, keeps that one.
`window.check()` issues a warning once per process, with both ways to keep the window, and changes nothing on the
machine.
[Why does my robot's upload get slow after a pause?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/why-does-my-robots-upload-get-slow-after-a-pause.md) has the
full table.

`python examples/components/window.py` printed:

```text
socket options this machine accepts: [(65535, 8, 1), (6, 16, 20), (6, 257, 5), (6, 258, 3)]
restarts a window after a pause: False
BBR on your own socket: False; its congestion control: None
pings in 0.3 s of idle time: 5
```

### `compress`: only where it saves time

```python
from sequence_ai.network import compress, msgpack_io

squeeze = compress.Squeeze()                                  # one per connection
body = msgpack_io.pack(squeeze.apply(observation))            # large arrays compressed in place, if that saves time
squeeze.uplink.note(len(body), seconds_the_upload_took)       # so it learns this link's upload rate
```

An array is compressed with zstd level 1 only while the upload time that saves, at the uplink rate measured on this
connection, exceeds the time to compress and decompress it. Data that does not compress, such as a JPEG's bytes, is sent
uncompressed and tried again later. Without the `zstandard` package (and before Python 3.14, which has zstd built in) it
uses zlib level 1.

**Measured.** Camera frames of 172,800 bytes (320 by 180, from a public robot dataset): 0.37 ms to compress, 0.21 ms
to decompress, about 1.9 times smaller, on a laptop. Those frames were decoded from video, which compresses better
than a camera's raw frames.

`python examples/components/compress.py` printed:

```text
a frame of 921,600 bytes was uploaded as 37,617
decompressed byte for byte: 884,137 bytes larger than what arrived
on that link the next frame is sent uncompressed: True
```

The example's frame is synthetic, flat regions and edges, so it compresses far more than a camera's does. The last
line shows the rule: once the link is fast enough that compressing costs more than it saves, the frame is sent
uncompressed.

### `frames`: a frame resized before upload, and decoded on the server

```python
from sequence_ai.network import frames

frame = frames.resize_image(camera.read(), 224, 224, mode="pad", filter="bilinear")
data = frames.encode(frame)            # a base64 JPEG
image = frames.decode(data)            # on the server: the HxWx3 uint8 array its policy reads
```

`"pad"` is openpi's `resize_with_pad`, byte for byte. The mode and the filter have no default and must be passed: a
policy sees what it was trained on. `frames.encode(frame)` gives a base64 JPEG for an input that carries its frames as
text, and `frames.image_size(data)` reads a frame's width and height from its header without Pillow. On the server,
`frames.decode(data)` turns that JPEG, or a PNG, back into the array, and returns an array it is given unchanged. It
opens no other format, since a picture comes over the network.

`python examples/components/frames.py` printed:

```text
pad: (224, 224, 3) with black rows at the top: True
stretch: (224, 224, 3)
encoded: 17,056 characters for 921,600 bytes; size from its header: (224, 224)
decoded: (224, 224, 3) uint8, 2.0 levels from the frame on average
```

### `wifi_power`: Wi-Fi power saving, detected

```python
from sequence_ai.network import wifi_power

wifi_power.check()    # the interface whose power saving is on, after warning how to disable it; else None
```

With power saving enabled, a Wi-Fi adapter sleeps between the access point's beacons, and a policy's response is
delayed until the adapter wakes. `check()` reads the machine's settings and changes nothing. Linux only.

`python examples/components/wifi_power.py` printed, on a Mac:

```text
Wi-Fi power saving is on: no (or this is not Linux, or not Wi-Fi)
```

### `connect`: the client-side components combined

```python
from sequence_ai.network import connect

with connect("http://your-gpu:8000", compress=True) as link:     # compress: only if your server decompresses
    response = link.act({"image": frame, "state": state})
    print(link.stats()["latency_us"]["act_us"])                   # the requests' p50, p95 and p99
```

One httpx connection with `window`'s socket options on it, a small GET while it is idle, msgpack both ways, and each
request timed. A ping and a request never run at once and never take a second connection: a client that starts a request
while a ping is in flight would open a new connection for it, with a new handshake and a cold window.

Your server needs a POST that takes a msgpack body and responds with msgpack or JSON, and any cheap GET for the
ping (`ping_path=None` disables the pings). [`examples/server.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/server.py) is one, and so is the
[Quickstart](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/quickstart.md)'s.

| Option | Default | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `act_path` | `"/act"` | the POST path the observation is sent to |
| `ping_path` | `"/ping"` | the GET sent while idle; `None` for no pings |
| `ping_every_s` | `0.1` | the idle time after which a ping is sent |
| `ping_for_s` | `60.0` | how long pings continue after the last request |
| `compress` | `False` | compress large arrays where that saves time; the server must call `compressed.expand` |
| `timeout` | `10.0` | seconds to wait for a response |
| `headers` | `None` | headers sent with every request |
| `check` | `True` | warn once if this machine restarts its window after a pause, and if Wi-Fi power saving is on |

**One connection, kept open.** This is one line in any client: create one `httpx.Client` and reuse it. Measured: a
new connection for each call took a median 305.9 ms; one reused connection, 121.0 ms. The handshake was 184.9 ms per
call. `connect()` keeps one.

## Server side

### `ping`: a server-side ping

```python
import websockets
from sequence_ai.network import ping

async with ping.serve(handler, host, port) as server:      # websockets' own server, with a ping every 100 ms
    await server.serve_forever()

async with websockets.serve(handler, host, port, **ping.websockets_options()):    # the same, as its options
    ...

uvicorn.run(app, **ping.uvicorn_options())                                         # the same, under uvicorn
```

A WebSocket library answers a ping with a pong by itself. A server that pings therefore makes the robot send a few
bytes each interval, and the robot's kernel never counts the connection idle. Nothing changes on the robot.

**Measured.**

- **Where it helped.** Between machines of one cloud provider, on RTTs of 11.7 and 69.2 ms, an upload after
  500 ms of silence took 3.0 round trips; with the server pinging every 100 ms it took 1.1 (100 KB and 500 KB) and
  1.25 (1 MB).
- **Where it did not.** On a home connection with a cellular uplink, about 36 ms from the GPU, 921,600-byte
  uploads after 10 s of silence took a median of 264 ms without the pings and 368 ms with them (six each,
  alternating).

A server that answers one HTTP request with one response cannot send anything unsolicited. There the ping comes from the
robot: `window.Warm`, which `connect()` applies to its connection.
[How do I keep a WebSocket policy server's connection warm?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-keep-a-websocket-policy-servers-connection-warm.md)
has the rest.

`python examples/components/ping.py` printed:

```text
response: observation
the server measured the connection's RTT from its pings: 0.17 ms
```

### `one_write`: a response in one write

```python
import uvicorn
from sequence_ai.network.one_write import WholeResponse, one_write_http

uvicorn.run(WholeResponse(app), http=one_write_http())
```

`app` is any ASGI app: FastAPI's and Starlette's too.

uvicorn writes a response in pieces. A tunnel or proxy in front of the server can delay every piece after the first
until the client has acknowledged the first, so each request takes one more round trip than necessary.

**Measured.** Behind such a tunnel, with a TCP connect of p50 89.5 ms: headers then body, GET p50 189.7 ms; the same
response in one write, 106.7 ms. Not measured on a direct connection, and the number of samples was not recorded.

`python examples/components/one_write.py` printed `response: b'ok'`.

### `tcp_link`: each client's link, read from the kernel

```python
from sequence_ai.network import tcp_link

tcp_link.read(sock)             # any connected socket
tcp_link.of(scope["client"])    # in an ASGI app served with one_write_http(): this request's own connection
```

Each returns `rtt_ms`, `rttvar_ms`, `retrans`, `total_retrans`, `cwnd` and, where the kernel provides it,
`delivery_kbps`; or `None` where the kernel provides none, as on macOS. A robot's own OS may not expose these to
the program that runs on it, and the server reads every robot the same way.

`python examples/components/tcp_link.py` printed, on a Mac:

```text
this connection, as the server's kernel reports it: None
```

### `compressed`: decompress what the client compressed

```python
from sequence_ai.network import compressed, msgpack_io

observation, grew = compressed.expand(msgpack_io.unpack(body), limit=64 << 20)
```

An item whose declared size is smaller than its decompressed size is rejected rather than decompressed past `limit`.

## Both sides

### `msgpack_io`

```python
from sequence_ai.network import msgpack_io

body = msgpack_io.pack({"image": frame, "state": joints})
observation = msgpack_io.unpack(body)
```

Bytes are sent as bytes and numpy arrays as their raw data, whereas JSON carries bytes as base64, a third larger on the
wire. It is plain Python, so neither side installs a msgpack package. It writes arrays as msgpack-numpy does and reads
openpi's layout as well. An object array is rejected: decoding one would run code chosen by the sender.

`python examples/components/msgpack_io.py` printed:

```text
150,670 bytes for an image of 150,528; content type application/x-seq-msgpack
arrays returned as arrays: (224, 224, 3) float32
```

### `latency_stats`

```python
from sequence_ai.network.latency_stats import LatencyStats, now_us

stats = LatencyStats(latencies=["request_us"])
sent = now_us(); ...; stats.since("request_us", sent)
stats.snapshot()["latency_us"]["request_us"]    # n, mean, max, p50, p95, p99
```

A percentile is `None` until its window contains enough samples for it: the p99 of 20 samples is only the largest of the
20. So p50 needs 2 samples, p95 needs 20 and p99 needs 100.

`python examples/components/latency_stats.py` printed:

```text
200 requests: p50 248 ms, p95 281 ms, p99 290 ms
```

## openpi and LeRobot

**openpi.** Keep openpi's client and server. On the GPU, start openpi's own server through this package: it then pings
each robot every 100 ms and hands its policy each picture sent as JPEG as the array it reads. On the robot, import
`image_tools` from here, so its pictures go as JPEG, and add the client-side components to the connection the client
holds.

```bash
uv run --with sequence-ai python -m sequence_ai.network.openpi scripts/serve_policy.py --env=DROID   # the GPU
```

```python
from openpi_client import websocket_client_policy
from sequence_ai.network import openpi
from sequence_ai.network.openpi import image_tools     # in place of openpi_client's: pictures go as JPEG

policy = websocket_client_policy.WebsocketClientPolicy(host, port)
kept = openpi.keep(policy)             # BBR and TCP keepalive on its socket; a WebSocket ping while it is idle
observation["observation/image"] = image_tools.resize_with_pad(frame, 224, 224)
action = policy.infer(observation)     # as before
```

In a server script of your own, `openpi.patch()` before it makes openpi's server does what the command does.

`keep()` is verified against openpi-client 0.1.2 on a local connection, and the server side and `image_tools` against
a server module built as openpi's `websocket_policy_server.py` is. Measured on a WebSocket connection of the kind
openpi's client holds, between two cloud machines: a 100 KB upload 0.53 s after each response took two to three round
trips without `keep()` and one with it ([Measurements](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md)). With openpi's own server and client, `keep()`
was measured in one closed-loop run ([the table](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md#openpikeep-with-openpis-own-server-and-client)), and
the pictures as JPEG with the server's pings in another
([the table](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md#pictures-as-jpeg-with-openpis-own-server-and-client)).
[How do I run π0 (openpi) on a remote GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-run-pi0-openpi-on-a-remote-gpu.md)

**LeRobot.** LeRobot 0.7.0's remote inference talks over Zenoh, which sends a frame on an idle link only every few
seconds. One setting makes it every 100 ms:

```python
from sequence_ai.network import lerobot

path = lerobot.keep_alive_file("zenoh-keep-alive.json5")
```

Give the file to both sides: the policy server reads it from `zenoh.config_file`, and the robot's remote inference
from `zenoh_config_path`.

Checked: Zenoh 1.10.2 takes the setting, and two idle peers on one machine then sent a frame every 102 ms each way.
Measured between two Zenoh peers on two cloud machines: a 100 KB request 0.53 s after each response took two to three
round trips without the file and one with it ([Measurements](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md)). Not tested
with LeRobot's own client and server.
[How do I reduce the latency of LeRobot remote inference?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-reduce-the-latency-of-lerobot-remote-inference.md)

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/faq.md

# FAQ: errors you may see, and what to do next

Each entry starts with what to do. The error text under it is the code's output when the error was reproduced
(macOS on Apple silicon, Python 3.12, sequence-ai 0.62.0, httpx 0.28, uvicorn 0.54), unless the entry states
otherwise.

Network layer (`sequence_ai.network`):

- [Installing](#installing)
- [Connecting](#connecting)
- [Sending and reading](#sending-and-reading)
- [With openpi and LeRobot](#with-openpi-and-lerobot)
- [On the server](#on-the-server)
- [What a component reports about your machine](#what-a-component-reports-about-your-machine)
- [A network component made nothing faster](#a-network-component-made-nothing-faster)

Inference layer (`sequence_ai.engine`):

- [`cuda_graphs`](#cuda_graphs)
- [`batcher`](#batcher)
- [`replicas`](#replicas)
- [`slack`](#slack)

[General](#general)

## Installing

### `ImportError: connect() uses httpx for its connection, and httpx is not installed`

httpx is a dependency of `sequence-ai`, so `pip install sequence-ai` installs it. The error appears where `link.py` was
copied into a project that has no httpx: install it there, as the error message states.

```text
ImportError: connect() uses httpx for its connection, and httpx is not installed: pip install httpx
```

### `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'numpy'` or `'uvicorn'`

The quickstart's two files import numpy, and its server runs under uvicorn:
`pip install "sequence-ai[server,arrays]"` installs both.

```text
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'numpy'
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'uvicorn'
```

numpy is optional for the components themselves. Without it, `connect()` and `msgpack_io` carry plain values, and an
array the server sent comes back as nested lists:

```text
{'state': [0.0, 1.0], 'prompt': 'pick'}
```

### `ImportError: resizing a frame needs Pillow, which is not installed here`

Pillow is a dependency of `sequence-ai`. The error appears where `frames.py` was copied into a project that has no
Pillow: `pip install pillow`. `frames.resize_image`, `frames.encode` and `frames.decode` use Pillow, and
`openpi.image_tools` and `openpi.patch()` through them; no other component does.

```text
ImportError: resizing a frame needs Pillow, which is not installed here: pip install pillow
ImportError: encoding an array or PIL image needs Pillow, and it is missing or broken here: pip install pillow. Pass an already-encoded base64 str or bytes to avoid it.
```

The first line is what `frames.resize_image` raises, the second what `frames.encode` raises.

### Which extra do I need?

| You use | Install |
|---|---|
| `connect()` on the robot, `frames`, `window`, `ping`, `tcp_link`, `wifi_power`, `msgpack_io`, `latency_stats`, `lerobot`, and every inference component | `sequence-ai`, nothing more |
| numpy arrays in observations or responses, `compress=True` | add `arrays`: `pip install "sequence-ai[arrays]"` |
| `one_write` under uvicorn on the GPU | add `server`: `pip install "sequence-ai[server]"` |
| `bench/`, the measuring tool | a checkout of the repository; it is standard library only |

Python 3.9 or later.

## Connecting

### `httpx.ConnectError: [Errno 61] Connection refused`

Nothing is listening at that address and port. Check, in this order:

1. The server is running, and its log shows the port you gave `connect()`.
2. The server listens on an address the robot can reach. `127.0.0.1` is reachable from the same machine only: on a
   GPU elsewhere, start it on `0.0.0.0` (`python quickstart_server.py 0.0.0.0 8000`).
3. The URL starts with `http://` and has the port: `connect("http://YOUR_GPU:8000")`.

```text
httpx.ConnectError: [Errno 61] Connection refused: no response from http://127.0.0.1:8000. Is the policy server running there, listening on an address this machine can reach (0.0.0.0, not 127.0.0.1, for another machine), on that port?
```

The text up to the first colon after `ConnectError:` comes from the operating system, so Linux prints a different
number. The rest comes from `connect()`, with the address it was given.

### `httpx.ConnectTimeout: timed out`

The address did not respond at all. That is the symptom of a closed firewall: the GPU's network drops the robot's
packets instead of refusing them. Open the server's port to the robot's address in the GPU's firewall, then try again.

```text
httpx.ConnectTimeout: timed out
```

It is raised after `timeout` seconds, 10 unless you pass another: `connect(url, timeout=2)`.

### `httpx.ConnectError: [Errno 8] nodename nor servname provided, or not known`

The host name in the URL does not resolve. Check the spelling, or use the GPU's IP address.

```text
httpx.ConnectError: [Errno 8] nodename nor servname provided, or not known
```

### `httpx.ReadTimeout: timed out`

The server took longer than `timeout` to respond: `connect(url, timeout=60)` waits a minute. A model's first call is
often its slowest, because it loads or compiles then. If every call is slow, the time is in the model and not in the
link: the `server-timing` header in the [quickstart's server](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/quickstart.md) reports how long the model took.

```text
httpx.ReadTimeout: timed out
```

## Sending and reading

### `httpx.HTTPStatusError: Client error '404 Not Found'`

The server has no POST at that path. `connect()` posts to `/act` unless told otherwise:
`connect(url, act_path="/infer")`, or `link.act(observation, path="/infer")` for one call.

```text
httpx.HTTPStatusError: Client error '404 Not Found' for url 'http://127.0.0.1:8012/infer'
```

### `httpx.HTTPStatusError: Server error '500 Internal Server Error'` after adding `compress=True`

The server does not decompress the arrays. Either add one line where it reads the body, or leave
`compress=True` off:

```python
observation, _ = compressed.expand(msgpack_io.unpack(body), limit=64 << 20)
```

The robot sees this:

```text
httpx.HTTPStatusError: Server error '500 Internal Server Error' for url 'http://127.0.0.1:8012/act'
```

and the server's log shows the model receiving a map where it expected an array:

```text
AttributeError: 'dict' object has no attribute 'mean'
```

### `MsgpackError: ... cannot be sent as msgpack`

The observation contains a type msgpack cannot encode. Send JSON-like values, bytes and numpy arrays; convert a set
to a list, and an object to a dict of its fields.

```text
MsgpackError: set cannot be sent as msgpack (JSON values, bytes and numpy arrays can)
```

### `MsgpackError: a numpy array of dtype object is not carried`

Give the array a numeric, bool or string dtype. An array of Python objects is refused on purpose: reading one back
would run code the sender chose.

```text
MsgpackError: a numpy array of dtype object is not carried: only plain numeric, bool and string dtypes are
```

### `MsgpackError: msgpack type 0xc1 is not read here`

The body is not msgpack that this reader takes: it is another format, it was cut short, or it uses a msgpack
extension type. Check the response's `content-type`. `connect()` reads `application/json` responses as JSON and
everything else as msgpack.

```text
MsgpackError: msgpack type 0xc1 is not read here (extension types and the unused code)
```

## With openpi and LeRobot

### `TypeError: this client keeps no WebSocket connection at _ws`

`openpi.keep()` takes openpi's own `WebsocketClientPolicy`, which holds its connection at `_ws`. Pass that object,
and not a wrapper around it such as an `ActionChunkBroker`.

```text
TypeError: this client keeps no WebSocket connection at `_ws` (openpi_client's WebsocketClientPolicy does): nothing to keep warm
```

### `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'openpi_client'`

Install openpi's client from openpi's repository (`packages/openpi-client`, `pip install -e .`).
`sequence_ai.network.openpi` adds to that client and does not replace it.

```text
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'openpi_client'
```

### `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'typing_extensions'` on importing `openpi_client`

`pip install typing_extensions`. openpi-client 0.1.0 imports it without listing it as a dependency, so a new
environment that contains only openpi's client may lack it; inside openpi's own environment it is already there.

```text
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'typing_extensions'
```

### My openpi client prints nothing and never returns

It is waiting for the server. While the connection is refused, openpi's client retries it every 5 seconds, and logs
`Waiting for server at ...` and `Still waiting for server...` at INFO level, which is hidden unless logging is set
up. So the server is not up yet, or the port is wrong. This is read from openpi's source
(`websocket_client_policy.py`); it was not made to happen here.

### `BBR on its socket: False`

Expected anywhere but Linux, and on Linux until the BBR module is loaded: `sudo modprobe tcp_bbr`. The keepalive
options and the ping while idle are on either way. On this Mac:

```text
BBR on its socket: False; TCP keepalive options accepted: 4
```

### Does the LeRobot setting need to be applied on both sides?

Yes, each side sends its own keep-alive frames. In LeRobot 0.7.0 the policy server reads it from `zenoh.config_file`
and the robot's remote inference from `zenoh_config_path`. Both names are from LeRobot's source; the file has not been
tested with LeRobot's own client and server. See
[How do I reduce the latency of LeRobot remote inference?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-reduce-the-latency-of-lerobot-remote-inference.md)

## On the server

### `[Errno 48] error while attempting to bind on address ('127.0.0.1', 8000): address already in use`

Another program has the port. Give the server and the robot another one:

```bash
python quickstart_server.py 127.0.0.1 8001
python quickstart_robot.py http://127.0.0.1:8001
```

```text
ERROR:    [Errno 48] error while attempting to bind on address ('127.0.0.1', 8000): [errno 48] address already in use
```

### My server's log fills with `GET /ping`

That is the robot keeping its connection warm: one small request for each 100 ms the connection is idle, for a
minute after the last request. Three in 0.35 seconds looked like this:

```text
INFO:     127.0.0.1:52970 - "GET /ping HTTP/1.1" 200 OK
INFO:     127.0.0.1:52970 - "GET /ping HTTP/1.1" 200 OK
INFO:     127.0.0.1:52970 - "GET /ping HTTP/1.1" 200 OK
```

To keep the pings and lose the lines, start uvicorn with `access_log=False`. To stop the pings, pass
`connect(url, ping_path=None)`; `ping_every_s` and `ping_for_s` change how often and for how long.

### Can the server ping instead, so the robot's code does not change?

Only over a WebSocket. A server that answers one HTTP request with one response cannot send anything unsolicited. See
[How do I keep a WebSocket policy server's connection warm?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-keep-a-websocket-policy-servers-connection-warm.md)

## What a component reports about your machine

### `UserWarning: this machine restarts a connection's send window after each pause`

Do one of the two things it names, once, on the robot. Both need root. `connect(url, check=False)` disables the
warning without changing anything. The text below is the package's own, printed on a Mac with the Linux state
simulated; it is issued on Linux only.

```text
UserWarning: this machine restarts a connection's send window after each pause (net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle is 1), so an upload of 0.3 MB sent after one takes several round trips. `sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle=0` keeps the window through pauses (a line in /etc/sysctl.d/ keeps it after a reboot), as does loading BBR (`sudo modprobe tcp_bbr`), which window.socket_options() then sets on your connections
```

[Why does my robot's upload get slow after a pause?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/why-does-my-robots-upload-get-slow-after-a-pause.md) explains it.

### `Wi-Fi power saving is on for wlan0`

Run the command it gives on the robot. The text is the package's own, printed here for an interface named `wlan0`; it
is issued on Linux only, when the robot's default route is a Wi-Fi interface with power saving enabled.

```text
Wi-Fi power saving is on for wlan0, so its adapter can delay this robot's packets while it sleeps; `sudo iw dev wlan0 set power_save off` disables it until the next reboot, and `wifi.powersave = 2` under [connection] in a file in /etc/NetworkManager/conf.d/ keeps it disabled
```

### `window.keep(sock)` returns `False`, `tcp_link.read(sock)` and `wifi_power.check()` return `None`

Expected off Linux: those three read or set things only the Linux kernel has. Nothing fails, and the rest works. On
this Mac:

```text
window.keep(sock): False | window.congestion_of(sock): None
window.restarts_after_idle(): False | window.check(): False
tcp_link.read(sock): None
wifi_power.check(): None
```

On Linux, `window.keep(sock)` is `False` until the kernel's BBR module is loaded (`sudo modprobe tcp_bbr`).

## A network component made nothing faster

What a network component saves depends on the link:

- On round-trip times (RTTs) of about 101 and 241 ms, a robot sending a request every 0.53 s took no extra round trip
  after its pauses with the default settings, so there was nothing for BBR or a ping to save.
- On a home connection with a cellular uplink, a server-side ping showed no benefit (a median of 264 ms
  without it, 368 ms with it, six uploads each).
- On loopback, or between two machines on one switch, a round trip costs almost nothing, so saving one saves almost
  nothing.

The README has the [results](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/README.md#results) and the [limitations](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/README.md#limitations).
[Measure your own link](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-measure-the-link-between-my-robot-and-my-gpu.md) before and after.

## `cuda_graphs`

Lines that begin `cuda graphs:` are printed, not raised: the model keeps running, in eager mode where it was not
graphed.

### `cuda graphs: no CUDA GPU available: nothing captured`

This machine has no CUDA GPU that torch can use, so the model is unchanged. That is the expected line on a laptop.
On a machine that has a GPU, check `torch.cuda.is_available()`: a CPU-only build of torch prints the same line.

### `cuda graphs: action_head.denoiser is not in this model: not captured`

The path names no attribute of your model. Paths are dotted attribute names from the model you passed, as
`cuda_graphs.modules_of(model)` lists them. Use the census to get the path instead of writing it by hand:

```python
census = cuda_graphs.Census(cuda_graphs.modules_of(model))
for _ in range(3):
    model(observation)
    census.end_act()
census.close()
print(census.candidates())        # [{'path': 'denoiser', 'calls': 10, 'ms': 1.05}]
```

The line is printed on a machine with no GPU too, so a mistyped path shows up on a laptop.

### `cuda graphs: ... is not a torch module: not captured`

The path names something that is not a `torch.nn.Module`: a function, a tensor, a list. Name the module that contains
it.

### `cuda graphs: ... runs in eager mode for one of its shapes: ...`

One shape of that module's inputs could not be graphed, and runs in eager mode from now on. The other shapes are
unaffected. The text after the colon gives the reason:

- `its capture failed (...)`: the module does something a CUDA graph cannot record, with torch's own error in
  parentheses. Naming a smaller module inside it often works.
- `its output is of a type a graph cannot return`: the module returns something other than tensors and plain
  values.
- `its graph's output differed from eager mode's`: the replay did not equal eager mode byte for byte, so it is not used.
  The check is working as intended, and that shape stays in eager mode.
- `cuda graphs need torch 2.4 or later`: older torch cannot swap the GPU's random generator while a capture runs,
  and a failed capture would corrupt your model's random noise. Nothing is captured. Upgrade torch.

### I installed it and nothing got faster

In order of likelihood:

1. **The module is called once per run.** The gain comes from the kernel launches across many calls. Run the census:
   `calls` is the number of calls per run.
2. **The model was not launch-bound.** A model whose GPU is already busy nearly all the time has no launch overhead
   to remove: π0.5 under JAX was 98% GPU-busy.
3. **Every call has a new shape.** Each new shape is captured once; a run of new shapes is a run of captures.
4. **It is running in eager mode.** Look for a `runs in eager mode` line above.

[How do I make a PyTorch robot policy faster without changing its outputs?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-make-a-pytorch-robot-policy-faster-without-changing-its-outputs.md)

## `batcher`

### `ValueError: sizes [2, 4] must include 1: a call that waits alone is a batch of 1, and a batch in which the model raised is re-run call by call`

Include 1 in the sizes: `Batcher(run, sizes=[1, 2, 4])`. A call that arrives alone must be dispatched as a batch of
one.

### `ValueError: the model returned 3 outputs for a batch of 4`

Your function must return one output for each input, in order. It is given a list and returns a list of the same
length.

### My batches are all of size 1

Calls are batched only while they wait. With an idle model and `wait_ms=0`, each call is dispatched as soon as it
arrives. Raise `wait_ms` slightly (the examples use 2 ms), or expect batches only when the model is busy.

## `replicas`

### `TypeError: load must be a function a new process can import: defined at a module's top level, not a lambda and not a function inside another`

Each replica starts in its own process and imports `load` by name. Move it to the top of a module:

```python
def load():                       # at the top of a module, not inside main() and not a lambda
    model = build_model()
    return model.infer            # what one call runs
```

### `ReplicaStartFailed: the model's load raised: ...`

Your `load` raised in the replica's process; the text after the colon is its error, and the exception's `traceback`
is the replica's. Run `load()` once in a plain script to see it directly.

### `ReplicaStartFailed: the model did not load within 900 s`

The replica did not finish loading in time. For a model that takes longer: `ReplicaPool(load, start_timeout=1800)`.

### `ReplicaDied: the replica died mid-call (exit code -9)`

The process has exited: killed, or out of memory (an exit code of -9 is SIGKILL, which is also what the Linux
out-of-memory killer sends). The pool replaces it, and the call that was running gets this error. `ReplicaError`, by
contrast, is your model's own exception: the replica is alive and takes the next call.

### `ReplicaDied: the call exceeded its ... s deadline: the replica was terminated`

A call took longer than the deadline you gave it. The replica is terminated and replaced, since a model stuck in a call
cannot be interrupted any other way.

### `PoolHalted: ...`

The pool stopped replacing replicas after three consecutive deaths (`deaths_in_a_row`), or it was closed; the text
after the colon states which. A model that dies on every call is not reloaded indefinitely. Fix the cause, and create
a new pool.

### `ValueError: 1 replicas and 2 devices: one device per replica, at least one replica`

`devices` has one entry for each replica: `ReplicaPool(load, replicas=2, devices=[0, 1])`.

### Two replicas on one GPU are no faster

That is what was measured:
[Should I run two replicas of a policy on one GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/should-i-run-two-replicas-of-a-policy-on-one-gpu.md)

## `slack`

### `SizeFailed`

`slack.measure` could not run your forward pass at one of the batch sizes you listed, for example a batch that does
not fit in GPU memory. The exception carries the size, the timings measured so far, and your forward pass's own
error. List only the sizes that run.

### A replica serves only one robot

The policy leaves no slack: its robot requests the next chunk only when the current one is fully executed, so there
is no time in which to wait for a batch. See "Limitations" in [`docs/slack.md`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/slack.md).

## General

### Does any of this change my policy's outputs?

No. `cuda_graphs` keeps a graph only when its output equals eager mode's byte for byte. `batcher` returns to each
call the output your model produced for it. `replicas` and `slack` do not modify the model. No network component
touches the model, and `compress` is lossless: the server gets back the bytes the robot built.
`frames.resize_image` and `frames.encode` do change pixels, which is their purpose, and only where you call them: the
resize mode and filter have no default, so you name the ones your policy was trained with. `openpi.image_tools` resizes
as openpi's own does and then sends JPEG, and a server started through `sequence_ai.network.openpi` hands the policy the
JPEG's pixels: at quality 95 they moved a π0.5 policy's actions by 5.9% on average over 50 real observations, about a
tenth of what the policy's own sampling noise moves them.

### Do I need a GPU to try it?

No. The tests and every example except `examples/check_on_a_gpu.py` run on a machine with no GPU.

### Does it work on Windows?

It is tested on Linux and macOS. `replicas` starts its processes with `spawn`, which is available on all three, but
nothing here is tested on Windows.

### Something else

Open an issue at <https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/issues> with a minimal script that reproduces it,
the full error text and the output of `python -c "import sys, platform; print(sys.version, platform.platform())"`.

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-get-a-gpu-near-my-robot.md

# How do I get a GPU near my robot?

Use any GPU the robot can reach: one you own, one from a cloud provider, or one rented near the robot. Whichever it is,
the robot's code changes in one line, the address it connects to, and the components in this repository are used on
that GPU in the same way.

```python
link = connect("http://ADDRESS:8000")       # the GPU's address
```

GPUs are in short supply, and few are near any given robot. [General Sequences](https://generalsequences.com) rents
them by location, with this package's `seq gpu` commands: you name a city, a GPU is started near it, and you have root
in a container on it.

```bash
seq gpu places san fr                                           # the US cities a place can be
seq gpu add --place "San Francisco, CA" --gpu L4 --port 8000    # one GPU near it, and the port your server listens on
seq gpu ssh <id>                                                # root in its container: start your policy server
seq gpu remove <id>                                             # ends it, and its disk with it
```

The port is open to the address `seq gpu add` was run from; `seq gpu allow <id> <the robot's address>` opens it to the
robot. This is a paid service, billed while the GPU runs. Everything else on this page, and every component, works the
same on any other GPU. [Its documentation](https://generalsequences.com/docs/gpus/) has the rest.

## Why near

A robot that requests its next actions from a remote GPU waits for the model and for the network, and the network's
share grows with distance. The inference layer (`sequence_ai.engine`) reduces the model's time, the network layer
(`sequence_ai.network`) removes round trips the connection does not need, and the distance itself depends on where the
GPU is.

## The same line, for each client

| Your robot uses | The line that changes |
|---|---|
| `sequence_ai.network.connect()` | `connect("http://ADDRESS:8000")` |
| The quickstart's robot | `python quickstart_robot.py http://ADDRESS:8000` |
| openpi's client | `WebsocketClientPolicy(host="ADDRESS", port=8000)` |
| LeRobot's remote inference | its `endpoint`, `tcp/ADDRESS:PORT` |

The inference components need no change on a new GPU:

```bash
pip install sequence-ai
python examples/check_on_a_gpu.py        # the capture, checked against eager mode on that GPU
```

## Before the robot connects

- **The server listens on every address.** `127.0.0.1` is reachable from the GPU itself only:
  `python quickstart_server.py 0.0.0.0 8000`.
- **The port is open to the robot.** A rented GPU's firewall usually admits no one until you open a port. Open the
  server's port to the address or range the robot connects from. If you open it to everyone, check credentials in your
  server.

## Then measure

A GPU nearer the robot shortens the RTT, and the network components remove round trips that are not needed at all.
Which of them help on the new link is something to measure:
[How do I measure the link between my robot and my GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-measure-the-link-between-my-robot-and-my-gpu.md)
The measuring tool's server listens on port 9000 by default, so open that port too.

## Tested

The client side was tested against a server at another address of the same machine:
`python quickstart_robot.py http://ADDRESS:8017` printed its three requests.

## See also

- [How do I serve a robot policy from my own GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-serve-a-robot-policy-from-my-own-gpu.md)
- [How do I run π0 (openpi) on a remote GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-run-pi0-openpi-on-a-remote-gpu.md)
- [How many robots can one GPU serve?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-many-robots-can-one-gpu-serve.md)

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-keep-a-websocket-policy-servers-connection-warm.md

# How do I keep a WebSocket policy server's connection warm?

Have the server ping each connection every 100 ms. A WebSocket library answers a ping with a pong by itself, so a
server that pings makes the robot send a few bytes each interval, and the robot's kernel never counts the connection
as idle. Nothing changes on the robot: not its program, and not its library.

With the `websockets` library:

```python
import websockets
from sequence_ai.network import ping

async with ping.serve(handler, host, port) as server:      # websockets' own server, with a ping every 100 ms
    await server.serve_forever()

async with websockets.serve(handler, host, port, **ping.websockets_options()):    # the same, as its options
    ...
```

openpi's own policy server is built on the `websockets` library. Started through `python -m sequence_ai.network.openpi`,
it pings each connection the same way, with no change to its files:
[How do I run π0 (openpi) on a remote GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-run-pi0-openpi-on-a-remote-gpu.md)

Under uvicorn:

```python
uvicorn.run(app, **ping.uvicorn_options())
```

```bash
pip install sequence-ai          # this component imports only the standard library, and websockets for ping.serve
```

`ping.websockets_options()` and `ping.uvicorn_options()` return plain options, so you can also write them out and
install nothing:

```text
ping.websockets_options()  ->  {'ping_interval': 0.1, 'ping_timeout': 20.0}
ping.uvicorn_options()     ->  {'ws_ping_interval': 0.1, 'ws_ping_timeout': 20.0}
```

Without them, `websockets` pings every 20 seconds (the default of its `serve` in version 17.4). That finds a dead
connection. It is far too slow to keep a connection from going idle between a robot's requests.

## Why it matters

On Linux, a connection that has sent nothing for longer than its retransmission timeout has its congestion window
restarted, so the robot's next observation can take more round trips to upload. What restarts it is the robot's own
silence, which is why a ping the robot must answer fixes it from the server side.
[Why does my robot's upload get slow after a pause?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/why-does-my-robots-upload-get-slow-after-a-pause.md) has the
mechanism in full.

## Try it

[`examples/components/ping.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/components/ping.py) starts a server with the options, connects one client
and leaves it idle for half a second:

```bash
pip install websockets
python examples/components/ping.py
```

```text
response: observation
the server measured the connection's RTT from its pings: 0.17 ms
```

The second line is a side benefit: each pong tells the server the connection's round-trip time (RTT), which `websockets`
keeps as `connection.latency`.

## Why 100 ms

The robot's silence must stay shorter than its retransmission timeout, which is about its RTT plus 200 ms.
A WebSocket server sends its next ping one interval after the last pong came back, so the robot is silent for the
interval plus one RTT. An interval under 200 ms is therefore sufficient on a link of any length, and at 100 ms a
ping that is lost still leaves the next one inside the limit.

Measured on an RTT of 11.7 ms: pings 190 ms apart still kept the window (an upload after a pause took 1.18
round trips), and pings 250 ms apart did not (2.04). Anything from 25 to 190 ms apart measured the same.

## What was measured

| Link | Upload | Without the ping | With it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Machines of one cloud provider, RTTs of 11.7 and 69.2 ms, 20 samples per cell | 100 KB after 500 ms of silence | 3.0 round trips | 1.1 |
| the same | 500 KB | 3.0 | 1.1 |
| the same | 1 MB | 3.0 | 1.25 |
| Two cloud machines, RTTs of 11, 21, 41 and 81 ms, 40 uploads per cell, over a WebSocket whose server has `ping.websockets_options()` | 100 KB, 0.53 s after each response | 3.3, 2.1, 2.0 and 2.0 round trips | 1.2, 1.1, 1.0 and 1.0 |
| A home connection with a cellular uplink, about 36 ms from the GPU, six uploads each, alternating | 921,600 bytes after 10 s of silence | a median of 264 ms | 368 ms: no benefit |

A window that the pings do not fill still shrinks. BBR on the robot keeps that one: `window.keep(sock)`, or
`connect()`. And a ping does not grow a window that packet loss has cut: with 1% loss, 31 and 35 of 40 uploads
still took one extra round trip with a ping from the client side, and none of 40 with BBR
([Measurements](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md#with-1-packet-loss)).

## When the server cannot ping

**A plain HTTP server.** A server that answers one HTTP request with one response has no way to send anything
unsolicited. There the ping comes from the robot. `connect()` does it by itself:

```python
from sequence_ai.network import connect

link = connect("http://YOUR_GPU:8000")     # a small GET after each 100 ms of idle time
```

**A WebSocket server you cannot change.** Ping from the client side, on the connection your client already holds.
With openpi's client it is one line, `openpi.keep(policy)`: see
[How do I run π0 (openpi) on a remote GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-run-pi0-openpi-on-a-remote-gpu.md) With your own `websockets`
client:

```python
from websockets.sync.client import connect as ws_connect
from sequence_ai.network import window

with ws_connect("ws://YOUR_GPU:8000") as ws:
    window.keep(ws.socket)                               # BBR on its socket, where the machine allows

    def ping() -> None:
        if not ws.ping().wait(5.0):                      # no pong in 5 s: the connection is gone
            raise TimeoutError("no pong")

    warm = window.Warm(ping)                             # a ping after each 100 ms of idle time
    ws.send(observation)
    response = ws.recv()
    warm.used()                                          # after each request and response
```

Run against a stand-in server on one machine, that client sent four pings in 0.45 seconds of idle time.

## Tested

- `tests/network/test_ping.py` starts a `websockets` server with the options and checks that it pings every interval and
  that one without them does not. It does the same under uvicorn.
- uvicorn 0.54 takes the options on its `auto`, `websockets-sansio` and `websockets` implementations. uvicorn 0.39's
  `websockets-sansio` sends no pings, so on an older uvicorn leave `ws` at `auto` or pass `ws="websockets"`.
- The first three rows of the table were taken with the tool in [`bench/`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/tree/main/bench), whose server pings on
  request, and not with a policy server.
- The WebSocket row was taken with [`bench/ws_bench.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/bench/ws_bench.py): a `websockets` server with the
  options, and no policy behind it. [What do the components save?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md) has every cell.

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-make-a-pytorch-robot-policy-faster-without-changing-its-outputs.md

# How do I make a PyTorch robot policy faster without changing its outputs?

Replay the module your policy calls many times per run, its denoiser, from CUDA graphs captured from its own eager
kernels. `cuda_graphs.install` does that in one call, and keeps a graph only when its output equals eager mode's byte
for byte. On GR00T N1.7 on an L4 this reduced a run from 224 ms to 146 ms (1.54 times faster) with exactly the same
actions. It gains nothing on a model that already fuses and graphs its kernels.

```python
from sequence_ai.engine import cuda_graphs

cuda_graphs.install(model, ["action_head.denoiser"])    # model.action_head.denoiser, graphed in place
model(observation)                                       # a new shape: run in eager mode, captured, checked
model(observation)                                       # replayed
```

Nothing else in your code changes. The module stays where it is in your model, the same object of the same class,
with its weights, its `state_dict` and its hooks unchanged. Only its `forward` is replaced.

## Why this is faster

A vision-language-action policy with a diffusion or flow action head calls its denoiser several times per inference.
In eager PyTorch at batch 1, each of those calls launches many small kernels one by one, and launch overhead
dominates: on GR00T N1.7 on an L4 the GPU was busy 41% of the time. A CUDA graph replays the same kernels as one
launch.

## Why the outputs do not change

A graph replays the same kernels that eager mode ran, in the same order, so its arithmetic is identical. A compiler
that fuses kernels changes the order of the arithmetic, and with it the outputs. The three were measured on the same
model and GPU:

| Approach | Speed | Outputs |
|---|---|---|
| `torch.compile(backend="cudagraphs")` | 1.00× (225 ms) | unchanged |
| `torch.compile`, inductor | 1.45× | changed: 0.0051 apart on average |
| `cuda_graphs` | 1.54× (224 ms to 146 ms) | exactly the same, on inputs it was not captured on |

GR00T N1.7, one L4, its DiT captured. One model and one GPU: **these are not numbers for your model.**

`cuda_graphs` verifies the equality instead of assuming it. Each new shape is run in eager mode once, captured, and
replayed on the same inputs; the graph is kept only if the two outputs are equal byte for byte. A shape whose capture
fails or differs runs in eager mode from then on, which is reported once.

## Which module to name

One that is called more than once per run with the same shapes. To find it, count the calls over a few runs:

```python
census = cuda_graphs.Census(cuda_graphs.modules_of(model))
for _ in range(3):
    model(observation)                                   # one inference, as your code makes it
    census.end_act()
census.close()
paths = [row["path"] for row in census.candidates()]    # the outermost and slowest first
cuda_graphs.install(model, paths[:1])
```

[`examples/graph_a_module.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/graph_a_module.py) does all of it on a small flow-style model, and runs on
a machine with no GPU, where it prints which module it would graph and leaves the model unchanged.

## Check it on your GPU

```python
torch.manual_seed(0)                                     # a policy that draws noise: the same noise for each run
eager = model(observation)
cuda_graphs.install(model, paths[:1])
torch.manual_seed(0)
model(observation)                                       # a new shape: captured, and checked against eager mode here
torch.manual_seed(0)
print(cuda_graphs.same(eager, model(observation)))       # True: a replayed run, byte for byte
cuda_graphs.ACTIVE = False                               # the same model in eager mode again, to compare timings
```

[`examples/check_on_a_gpu.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/check_on_a_gpu.py) runs the capture on a real GPU and compares every
output with eager mode's. On a T4, its small flow-style model went from 16.1 ms to 2.4 ms per run: byte for byte on
inputs the capture never saw, the model's random noise unchanged, a new batch size captured automatically.

## What it is safe against

- **A graph whose output differs is never used.**
- **A failed capture does not change your model's random noise.** The GPU's random generator is swapped for a clone
  while a capture runs, and restored afterwards.
- **What your model checks about its module still holds:** `isinstance`, its type, its methods and its hooks, which
  fire around a replayed call too.

## Limitations

- **A model that already fuses and graphs its kernels.** π0.5 under JAX was 98% GPU-busy: there is no launch overhead
  left to remove. `cuda_graphs` is for PyTorch.
- **A module called once per run.** There is one launch sequence to save, not many.
- **Shapes that keep changing.** Each new shape is captured and checked once. A model whose shapes differ on every
  call spends its time capturing. A prompt of a new length is a new shape, captured the first time it occurs.
- **No CUDA GPU.** Nothing is graphed, which is reported once, and the model runs as before.
- **torch before 2.4.** It cannot swap the GPU's random generator during a capture, so nothing is captured.
- **Measured on two models.** Only GR00T N1.7's DiT and a small test model have been captured this way. LeRobot's
  policies and openpi's PyTorch models have not been tested with it:
  [How do I use the inference components with openpi, LeRobot or GR00T?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-use-the-inference-components-with-openpi-lerobot-or-gr00t.md)
  TensorRT and other compilers were not compared.

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-measure-the-link-between-my-robot-and-my-gpu.md

# How do I measure the link between my robot and my GPU?

Run one file where the GPU is and one where the robot is. The client prints how many round trips an upload takes after a
pause, with a ping through the pause, back to back, and as a camera stream. That tells you which network components
help on your link and which do not.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai && cd sequence-ai     # on both machines
python3 bench/server.py --port 9000                        # where the GPU is
python3 bench/client.py --host GPU_ADDRESS --port 9000     # where the robot is
```

Both files are standard library only and run on Linux and macOS. Nothing needs installing, and no model is involved.
With the defaults a run takes about 100 seconds plus the time the uploads take on your link.

## What it prints

This is a run of the defaults with both ends on one machine. Loopback involves no network, so these numbers indicate
nothing about any link. They are here to show the table's format.

```text
host 127.0.0.1  handshake 0.2 ms  baseline rtt min 0.1 / p50 0.2 ms  congestion None
mode            size    p50 ms    p95 ms    p99 ms   x rtt
idle          100000       0.3       0.5         -    1.54
ping          100000       0.2       0.3         -    1.04
continuous    100000       0.0       0.1         -    0.20
idle          500000       0.2       0.4         -    1.14
ping          500000       0.3       0.4         -    1.29
continuous    500000       0.1       0.1         -    0.55
idle         1000000       0.4       0.7         -    2.09
ping         1000000       0.3       0.6         -    1.69
continuous   1000000       0.2       0.3         -    1.14
30Hz           50000       0.2       0.3       0.3    1.00
10Hz          100000       0.2       0.3       0.3    1.19
10Hz          500000       0.3       0.5       0.6    1.29
```

- **The first line** is the link itself: how long the TCP handshake took, the round-trip time (RTT) with no data on it
  (`baseline`), and the congestion control the connection uses (`None` where the system does not report it, as on
  macOS).
- **`mode`** is what was sent, and **`size`** how many bytes each upload had.
- **`p50`, `p95`, `p99`** are how long an upload took to be acknowledged. `p99` is given for streams only, which have
  enough frames for it.
- **`x rtt`** is the median over the baseline RTT: how many round trips an upload took. This is the column to
  read.

It also writes `result.json` with every sample and the kernel's state of the connection around each upload.

## What each block sends

| Block | What it sends | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| `baseline` | an empty frame and its ack | the RTT with no data on it |
| `idle` | a frame, then a pause, then the next | what a pause between uploads costs |
| `ping` | as `idle`, the server pinging through the pause | whether a ping from the server side keeps the window |
| `keepwarm` | as `idle`, the robot sending a byte through the pause | the same, done from the client side |
| `continuous` | the next frame as soon as the last is acknowledged | the upload with a warm window |
| `stream` | frames at a fixed rate, acks not waited for | what each frame of a camera stream costs |
| `twowrite` | a frame in two writes with Nagle on | what a header and a body written apart cost |

The defaults run `idle`, `ping`, `continuous` and `stream`, with uploads of 100 KB, 500 KB and 1 MB, 500 ms of
silence, a ping every 100 ms, and 20 samples of each.

## How to read your result

| You see | It means | What to add |
|---|---|---|
| `idle` near 2 or 3, `continuous` near 1 | A pause costs your uploads extra round trips | A ping or BBR: the next two rows show which |
| `ping` or `keepwarm` near 1 | A ping through the pause keeps the window | `connect()` on the robot, or [`ping`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-keep-a-websocket-policy-servers-connection-warm.md) on a WebSocket server |
| `ping` no better than `idle` | A ping does not help on this link | Run again with `--bbr`; if that is near 1, use `window` |
| `idle` and `continuous` both near 1 | The pause costs nothing here | Nothing for the pause |
| `stream` rows well above 1 | Frames wait on the link: loss, or the last hop | Look at the last hop first: `wifi_power.check()` on the robot |
| A large `baseline` | The GPU is far away | [A GPU nearer the robot](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-get-a-gpu-near-my-robot.md) |

## Match the run to your robot

The defaults measure large uploads after half a second of silence. To measure what your robot sends, give its sizes
and its pace:

```bash
# a robot that acts every 0.53 s with 24 KB of frames: the pause, a ping from each side, then BBR
python3 bench/client.py --host HOST --sizes 24k --idle-ms 530 --samples 40 --modes idle,ping,keepwarm --warm 1m
python3 bench/client.py --host HOST --sizes 24k --idle-ms 530 --samples 40 --modes idle --warm 1m --bbr
```

| Flag | What it sets | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `--sizes` | frame sizes for `idle`, `ping`, `keepwarm` and `continuous` | `100k,500k,1m` |
| `--idle-ms` | the silence after each ack | `500` |
| `--ping-ms` | the interval of the pings and of the robot's bytes | `100` |
| `--stream` | camera streams, as `HZxSIZE` | `30x50k,10x100k,10x500k` |
| `--seconds` | how long each stream runs | `10` |
| `--samples` | samples for each block and size | `20` |
| `--modes` | the blocks to run, in order | `idle,ping,continuous,stream` |
| `--bbr` | request BBR on this connection's socket | off |
| `--warm` | upload one frame of this size before measuring | none |
| `--out` | where the samples are written | `result.json` |

## Try other distances from one pair of machines

On Linux, as root, where the client sends from:

```bash
sudo tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 80ms          # about 80 ms more on the round trip
sudo tc qdisc change dev eth0 root netem delay 80ms loss 1%
sudo tc qdisc del dev eth0 root
```

## Reference measurements

| Link | Upload | After 500 ms of silence | Server pinging every 100 ms | One after another |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Three machines of one cloud provider, RTTs of 11.7 and 69.2 ms, 20 samples per cell | 100 KB | 3.0 round trips | 1.1 | 1.05 |
| the same | 500 KB | 3.0 | 1.1 | 1.1 |
| the same | 1 MB | 3.0 | 1.25 | 1.3 |

And two results that differed:

- **A home connection.** A robot on a home connection with a cellular uplink, about 36 ms from the GPU, uploading
  921,600 bytes after 10 s of silence, six uploads each way: a median of 264 ms without the server's pings and 368 ms
  with them. The pings showed no benefit.
- **The last hop.** On the same line, a laptop with its Wi-Fi settings page open scanned for networks every 20
  seconds, and a 30 Hz stream of 50 KB frames went from a median of 43 ms per frame to 181 ms while it scanned.

[`bench/README.md`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/bench/README.md) has these in full, and
[Why does my robot's upload get slow after a pause?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/why-does-my-robots-upload-get-slow-after-a-pause.md) has the
table for a robot that sends two requests per second.

## Measure a server that is already running

The tool above measures the link with its own server. To see the link while your policy server runs, read it off the
server's kernel (Linux):

```python
from sequence_ai.network import tcp_link

tcp_link.read(sock)             # any connected socket: rtt_ms, rttvar_ms, retrans, total_retrans, cwnd
tcp_link.of(scope["client"])    # in an ASGI app served with one_write_http(): this request's own connection
```

and on the robot, `link.stats()["latency_us"]["act_us"]` gives each request's p50, p95 and p99 as the robot saw them.

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-reduce-the-latency-of-lerobot-remote-inference.md

# How do I reduce the latency of LeRobot remote inference?

Start with the link, because LeRobot 0.7's remote inference already manages the robot's timing itself: put the
policy server near the robot, measure the link, and keep the link from going idle between observations. `sequence-ai`
has one small component for the last of these, a Zenoh setting, and it is the only thing here that touches LeRobot.

```python
from sequence_ai.network import lerobot

path = lerobot.keep_alive_file("zenoh-keep-alive.json5")     # an idle link then sends a frame every 100 ms
```

```bash
pip install sequence-ai          # it needs neither LeRobot nor Zenoh to write the file
```

Give the file to both sides, since each side sends its own frames:

| Side | LeRobot's setting | As a flag |
|---|---|---|
| The GPU: `lerobot-policy-server` | `zenoh.config_file` | `--zenoh.config_file=zenoh-keep-alive.json5` |
| The robot: `lerobot-rollout --inference.type=remote` | `zenoh_config_path` | `--inference.zenoh_config_path=zenoh-keep-alive.json5` |

The setting names are read from LeRobot 0.7.0's source (`ZenohConfig.config_file` in `transport/zenoh.py`,
`RemoteInferenceConfig.zenoh_config_path` in `inference/factory.py`). The flags follow from them the way LeRobot's
other flags do.

## Tested

- **Verified:** Zenoh 1.10.2 takes the setting. With the file, an idle link between two Zenoh peers on one machine sent
  a frame about every 100 ms each way; without it, a frame every 1.5 s or less often. `tests/network/test_lerobot.py`
  repeats this when Zenoh is installed.
- **From source inspection:** LeRobot loads `config_file` first and then sets only its own keys over it (the
  mode, the endpoints, discovery, shared memory and the connect timeout), so a transport setting written in the file
  stays.
- **Measured on a real link:** two Zenoh peers on two cloud machines, one answering the
  other's requests. A 100 KB request 0.53 s after each response took 38.1, 44.8, 82.8 and 164.3 ms at round-trip times
  (RTTs) of 11, 21, 41 and 81 ms, and 13.9, 23.2, 42.3 and 82.2 ms with the file on both ends: two to three round trips
  became one, on 40 of 40 requests. [What do the network components save?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md) has the table.

## Limitations

- The file has not been tested with LeRobot's own policy server and robot: the measurement used two Zenoh peers.
- On some links the idle restart costs nothing: see [the README's limitations](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/README.md#limitations).

## Try it

[`examples/quickstart_lerobot.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/quickstart_lerobot.py) writes the file and prints where to set it on each
side:

```bash
python examples/quickstart_lerobot.py
```

```text
wrote zenoh-keep-alive.json5:
{
  "transport": {
    "link": {
      "tx": {
        "keep_alive": 100
      }
    }
  }
}
on the GPU, the policy server's setting:   zenoh.config_file = zenoh-keep-alive.json5
on the robot, remote inference's setting:  zenoh_config_path = zenoh-keep-alive.json5
```

`keep_alive` is how many keep-alive frames a Zenoh link sends in one lease. The lease is 10 seconds unless you
changed it, so 100 frames per lease is one every 100 ms. The lease itself is unchanged: it is how long a silent peer
is waited for, and a short one drops a robot whose Wi-Fi stalls for a moment.

**You already have a Zenoh file**, for TLS or access control. LeRobot takes one file, so put both in it:

```python
mine = {"transport": {"link": {"tls": {"root_ca_certificate": "ca.pem"}}}}
path = lerobot.keep_alive_file("zenoh.json5", base=mine)     # your settings, with the keep-alive beside them
```

Zenoh 1.10.2 loaded that file with both settings in it.

## Why an idle link costs anything

On Linux, a TCP connection that has sent nothing for longer than its retransmission timeout, which is at least its
RTT plus 200 ms, has its congestion window restarted. The next observation can then take more round trips to upload
than it would on a warm connection. A link that sends a small frame every 100 ms is never idle that long.
[Why does my robot's upload get slow after a pause?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/why-does-my-robots-upload-get-slow-after-a-pause.md) has the
measurements, including the links where the pause cost nothing.

## The other things that set the latency

**The distance.** The RTT between robot and GPU is incurred on every request, whatever else is done.
