[Measure it](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-measure-the-link-between-my-robot-and-my-gpu.md), and if the GPU is far,
[get one nearer](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-get-a-gpu-near-my-robot.md).

**LeRobot's own settings.** These are LeRobot's, from the `RemoteInferenceConfig` of 0.7.0, and were not measured
here:

| Setting | Default | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `encoding` | `"raw"` | `"jpeg"` sends camera frames as JPEG, at `jpeg_quality` (90), which makes each upload smaller |
| `refill_seconds` | `0.5` | Request the next chunk when this much playback is left; never less than the recent longest turnaround plus one action interval |
| `chunk_merge` | `"auto"` | How a new chunk is merged with the one being executed: `"append"` or `"aligned"` |
| `max_observation_age_s` | `5.0` | The oldest observation that is still acted on |

**The robot's machine.**

- `window.keep()` sets BBR on one socket. It cannot reach LeRobot's sockets, because Zenoh opens its own.
  The machine-wide settings do reach them, and both need root:
  `sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=bbr` (after `sudo modprobe tcp_bbr`), or
  `sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle=0`.
- On Wi-Fi, check power saving. This reads the machine's settings and changes nothing:

  ```python
  from sequence_ai.network import wifi_power

  wifi_power.check()    # the interface whose power saving is on, having warned how to turn it off; else None
  ```

## What this package does not add to LeRobot

LeRobot's remote inference has its own transport, message format and client, so `connect()`, `msgpack_io`,
`compress` and `one_write` do not apply to it. LeRobot already requests the next chunk ahead of time based on
the turnaround it measured, aligns a new chunk with the one being executed, and can send frames as JPEG.
[The comparison page](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/comparison.md) describes what each does, from source.

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-run-pi0-openpi-on-a-remote-gpu.md

# How do I run π0 (openpi) on a remote GPU?

Run openpi's own policy server on the GPU and openpi's own client on the robot, as openpi's guide describes.
`sequence-ai` then changes the command that starts the server, and two lines on the robot: the server pings each robot
and takes its pictures as JPEG, and the robot sends them that way and keeps its connection from going idle between
action chunks.

On the GPU, in openpi's repository. openpi's `docs/remote_inference.md` starts the server with
`uv run scripts/serve_policy.py --env=DROID`, on port 8000; this runs the same script, unchanged:

```bash
uv run --with sequence-ai python -m sequence_ai.network.openpi scripts/serve_policy.py --env=DROID
```

On the robot:

```python
from openpi_client import websocket_client_policy
from sequence_ai.network import openpi
from sequence_ai.network.openpi import image_tools      # was: from openpi_client import image_tools

policy = websocket_client_policy.WebsocketClientPolicy(host="YOUR_GPU", port=8000)
kept = openpi.keep(policy)                               # keeps the connection warm
observation["observation/exterior_image_1_left"] = image_tools.resize_with_pad(frame, 224, 224)    # now a JPEG
action_chunk = policy.infer(observation)["actions"]     # openpi's own call, unchanged
```

```bash
pip install sequence-ai          # on the robot: no extra needed. The GPU's command above brings its own.
```

π0 and π0.5 are the models; openpi is the repository that serves them. Nothing of openpi's is replaced here: the
client, the server, the msgpack layout and the responses stay openpi's own. A server started this way serves a robot
that sends arrays as before, and `keep()` needs nothing of the server; a robot that sends its pictures as JPEG needs the
server started this way.

## What the lines do

| Line | What it does | When it applies |
|---|---|---|
| `python -m sequence_ai.network.openpi`, on the GPU | openpi's server pings each connection every 100 ms, and hands its policy each picture sent as JPEG as the array it reads | always; a picture sent as an array reaches the policy as before |
| `image_tools` from `sequence_ai.network.openpi`, on the robot | `resize_with_pad` fits each picture exactly as openpi's does, then returns it as base64 JPEG at quality 95; `convert_to_uint8` returns that as it is | always; the server must be started as above |
| `openpi.keep(policy)`, on the robot | BBR as the socket's congestion control | Linux, with the kernel's BBR module loaded (`sudo modprobe tcp_bbr`) |
| | TCP keepalive | every machine that takes the options |
| | A WebSocket ping each 100 ms the connection is idle, for 60 s after the last `infer()` | always |

A robot that executes an action chunk before requesting the next one leaves its connection silent in between. On
Linux, a connection silent for longer than its retransmission timeout has its congestion window restarted, so the
next observation can take more round trips to upload.
[Why does my robot's upload get slow after a pause?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/why-does-my-robots-upload-get-slow-after-a-pause.md) has the
mechanism and the links where it did and did not cost anything. The pings keep the connection from going silent while
the server can answer them; openpi's server answers none while it runs inference, so on a Linux robot without BBR the
window can still be halved once before each upload ([measurements](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md)). BBR on the robot avoids that.
JPEG makes the upload itself smaller: two 224 x 224 pictures are 301,056 bytes as arrays.

`kept.bbr` reports whether the socket accepted BBR, `kept.congestion` which congestion control it now uses, and
`kept.warm.pings` how many pings were answered. `kept.close()` stops the pings; the connection stays openpi's.

In a server script of your own, call `openpi.patch()` before it makes openpi's `WebsocketPolicyServer`: that is what the
command does before it runs `scripts/serve_policy.py`.

## Try it without a GPU or a checkpoint

[`examples/quickstart_openpi.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/quickstart_openpi.py) starts a stand-in server on your machine that
speaks openpi's protocol, then runs openpi's real client against it with the one line added. It needs openpi's client
(`packages/openpi-client` in openpi's repository, `pip install -e .`).

```bash
python examples/quickstart_openpi.py
```

Run in a new environment with sequence-ai 0.62.0 and openpi-client 0.1.2, on a Mac, it printed:

```text
BBR on its socket: False; TCP keepalive options accepted: 4
infer 0: a chunk of 10 actions
infer 1: a chunk of 10 actions
infer 2: a chunk of 10 actions
pings answered while it was idle: 12
```

Twelve pings is four in each of the three half-second pauses. BBR is `False` because a Mac has none.

Against a real openpi server, [`examples/openpi_robot.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/openpi_robot.py) takes its host and port.

## Tested

- **Verified:** `openpi.keep()` against openpi-client 0.1.2 on a local connection, as above and in
  `tests/network/test_openpi.py`.
- **Verified:** the server's pings and its decoding, and `image_tools`, against a server module built as openpi's
  `websocket_policy_server.py` is, on a local connection; and the command, against a script run as
  `scripts/serve_policy.py` is (`tests/network/test_openpi_server.py`).
- **Measured on a real link:** `keep()` on a WebSocket connection of the kind openpi's client
  holds (the `websockets` library on both ends, compression off, a stand-in for the client class), between two cloud
  machines. A 100 KB upload 0.53 s after each response took 37.6, 44.4, 82.4 and 163.8 ms at round-trip times (RTTs) of
  11, 21, 41 and 81 ms, and 12.7, 22.7, 41.8 and 82.6 ms with `keep()`: two to three round trips became one, on 40 of 40
  uploads. [What do the network components save?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md) has the table.
- **Measured with openpi's own server and client:** one closed-loop run with π0.5 (`pi05_droid`) on an L4, the client in
  a Linux virtual machine on a home connection, 301 KB per request. The time a request spent outside inference had a
  median of 181 and 152 ms in two episodes without `keep()`; with it, 92 ms in an episode without packet loss and 157 ms
  in one that lost packets; with the BBR module loaded as well, 86 and 91 ms.
  [The table](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md#openpikeep-with-openpis-own-server-and-client) has the idle times and the congestion
  window.
- **Measured with openpi's own server and client, the pictures as JPEG:** one closed-loop run with π0.5 on an L4, the
  robot a simulated arm on a Mac on a home connection, the server pinging. Each request's upload went from 301.5 KB to
  18.8 KB, and the time it spent outside the server, beyond one RTT, from about 97 to about 21 ms at the median.
  [The table](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md#pictures-as-jpeg-with-openpis-own-server-and-client).

## Limitations

- With openpi's own policy server, `keep()` has been measured on one link only: two 45 s episodes per setting, from a
  Linux virtual machine on a home connection. In the episode that lost packets it was no better than without it.
- The pictures as JPEG have been measured in one episode, against one with arrays, and together with the server's
  pings: the two were not measured apart.
- In that run the server took about 20 ms longer for each inference than when openpi's own command started it, with or
  without the pings and the decoding. It was started through another script, as `python -m` starts it, and why that
  costs time is not known. `openpi.patch()` in a server script of your own starts nothing through another script; it
  has not been measured.
- A JPEG is not the frame it was made from: at quality 95 it moved a π0.5 policy's actions by 5.9% on average over 50
  real observations, about a tenth of what the policy's own sampling noise does
  ([`frames.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/frames.py) has the measurement).
- `patch()` changes openpi's server through its module's `_server` and its `WebsocketPolicyServer`, as openpi's
  `websocket_policy_server.py` has them: a version built otherwise is refused with a `TypeError`, not changed.
- The README's [limitations](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/README.md#limitations) list the links where the idle restart costs nothing.

## What openpi already does

openpi's client and server already do several things a remote policy needs, so this package has no component for them:

- **One connection, kept open.** The client connects once and reuses the WebSocket for every `infer()`.
- **Arrays as raw bytes.** Observations and responses are sent as msgpack with numpy arrays as raw bytes.
- **Images resized on the robot.** openpi's guide resizes each image on the client with
  `image_tools.resize_with_pad(img, 224, 224)` before sending it, as an array.
- **Action chunks executed open-loop.** `ActionChunkBroker` requests a new chunk only when the current one is
  exhausted.

If you write your own server or client for an openpi model, `msgpack_io` reads openpi's array layout,
`frames.resize_image(..., mode="pad", filter="bilinear")` is openpi's `resize_with_pad`, byte for byte, and
`frames.decode` turns a picture sent as JPEG back into its array. [The comparison page](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/comparison.md) sets the two
side by side.

## If something fails

- `TypeError: this client keeps no WebSocket connection at _ws`: pass the `WebsocketClientPolicy` itself to
  `keep()`, not an `ActionChunkBroker` wrapped around it. Keep the broker for `infer()`.
- `RuntimeError: Error in inference server:` on the robot, after its pictures went as JPEG: the server was started
  without `sequence_ai.network.openpi`, so its policy was handed the pictures as text. Start it with the command above,
  or import `image_tools` from `openpi_client` again.
- `ValueError: observation/...: not a JPEG or PNG image` in the server's traceback: a picture under that key came as
  text or bytes that are not one. Send it as `image_tools` makes it, or as an array.
- `TypeError: this server is not built as openpi's websocket_policy_server.py is`: the openpi on the GPU starts its
  server another way than `patch()` was written for. Start it with openpi's own command, and send arrays.
- `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'typing_extensions'` on importing `openpi_client`: openpi-client 0.1.0 imports
  it without listing it as a dependency, so a new environment may lack it. `pip install typing_extensions`.
- The client prints nothing and never returns: while the connection is refused it retries every 5 seconds, so the
  server is not up yet or the port is wrong. This is read from openpi's source, not made to happen here.

More in the [FAQ](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/faq.md#with-openpi-and-lerobot).

## Where the GPU comes from

Any GPU the robot can reach on port 8000. [How do I get a GPU near my robot?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-get-a-gpu-near-my-robot.md)
covers the case where you have none nearby. The robot's code changes in one place: the `host`.

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-serve-a-robot-policy-from-my-own-gpu.md

# How do I serve a robot policy from my own GPU?

Put your model behind a small HTTP server on the GPU and call it from the robot with `connect()`. Everything here is
open source and runs on a GPU you already have: no account and no service of ours is involved.

On the GPU:

```bash
pip install "sequence-ai[server,arrays]"
python quickstart_server.py 0.0.0.0 8000
```

On the robot:

```python
from sequence_ai.network import connect

link = connect("http://YOUR_GPU:8000")                    # BBR, TCP keepalive, a ping when idle, msgpack: all on
actions = link.act({"image": frame, "state": state})["actions"]
```

[`quickstart_server.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/quickstart_server.py) is one short file with a function named `policy` that you
replace with your model. The [Quickstart](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/quickstart.md) runs both sides on one machine first, with the output of each
step. Run between two addresses of one machine, the robot printed:

```text
request 0: 8 actions of 7 numbers, the first [128. 128. 128.]
request 1: 8 actions of 7 numbers, the first [128. 128. 128.]
request 2: 8 actions of 7 numbers, the first [128. 128. 128.]
3 requests, the slowest took 4.8 ms
```

## You already have a server

Keep it. `connect()` needs two things from a server: a POST that takes a msgpack body and responds with msgpack or
JSON, and any cheap GET for its ping. In a FastAPI app that is two handlers, and two more names where uvicorn starts:

```python
import asyncio

import numpy as np
import uvicorn
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request, Response

from sequence_ai.network import compressed, msgpack_io
from sequence_ai.network.one_write import WholeResponse, one_write_http

app = FastAPI()


def policy(observation: dict) -> np.ndarray:
    return np.full((8, 7), float(observation["image"].mean()), dtype=np.float32)      # your model here


@app.post("/act")
async def act(request: Request) -> Response:
    observation, _ = compressed.expand(msgpack_io.unpack(await request.body()), limit=64 << 20)
    actions = await asyncio.to_thread(policy, observation)          # the model runs off the event loop
    return Response(msgpack_io.pack({"actions": actions}), media_type=msgpack_io.MEDIA_TYPE)


@app.get("/ping")
async def ping() -> Response:
    return Response()                                               # all the robot's ping needs: an empty response


if __name__ == "__main__":
    uvicorn.run(WholeResponse(app), host="127.0.0.1", port=8000, http=one_write_http())
```

This file was run with FastAPI 0.163 against the quickstart's robot: three requests answered, and with
`connect(url, compress=True)` three more, with three pings between them.

Your paths can have other names: `connect(url, act_path="/infer", ping_path="/healthz")`.

## You already have a client

Keep that too, and take single components. Each is one file and imports no other component:

```python
import httpx
from sequence_ai.network import window

transport = httpx.HTTPTransport(socket_options=window.socket_options())    # BBR and TCP keepalive, where it can
client = httpx.Client(base_url="http://YOUR_GPU:8000", transport=transport)

warm = window.Warm(ping=lambda: client.get("/ping"))     # a ping while the connection is idle
warm.used()                                              # call it each time you send on the connection
```

Run against the quickstart's server, those lines sent four pings in 0.45 seconds of idle time. One thing `connect()`
does that your own client must do itself: never let a ping and a request run at the same time. An HTTP/1.1 client
that starts a request while a ping is in flight opens a second connection for it, with a new handshake and a cold
window. `connect()` uses one connection and a lock; [`link.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/link.py) is short enough to read.

[`examples/components/`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/tree/main/examples/components) has a runnable file for each component, and
[Components](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/components.md) describes what each one does, what it needs and what was measured.

## Which components help on your link

A component saves time only on a link that has the cost it removes. Measure before you add:

| On your link | Add | Measured |
|---|---|---|
| A short round-trip time (round-trip time (RTT), about 21 ms) and pauses between requests | `connect()`, or `window` on your own client | 40 of 40 requests took one extra round trip without BBR, none with it |
| A longer RTT (about 101 or 241 ms), no loss | nothing for the pauses | 0 or 1 of 40 requests took an extra round trip with the default settings |
| A tunnel or proxy in front of the server | `one_write` | GET p50 189.7 ms with headers and body written apart, 106.7 ms in one write; not measured on a direct connection |
| Large raw arrays on a slow uplink | `compress=True` and `compressed.expand` | 172,800-byte frames came out about 1.9 times smaller for 0.37 ms |
| A new connection for each call | keep one open, as `connect()` does | 305.9 ms per call with a new connection, 121.0 ms reusing one |

The conditions behind each row are in the [README](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/README.md#results).
[How do I measure the link between my robot and my GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-measure-the-link-between-my-robot-and-my-gpu.md)
shows how to get the same numbers for your own link.

## Before a robot depends on it

- **Credentials.** The quickstart's server checks none. Open its port only to your robot's address, or check a header
  in your handler: `connect(url, headers={"authorization": "..."})` sends one with every request.
- **Timeout.** `connect()` waits 10 seconds for a response. A model that loads or compiles on its first call needs more:
  `connect(url, timeout=60)`.
- **Several robots on one GPU.** One request at a time is one forward pass each. The inference layer has `batcher`,
  which batches the waiting requests into one call to the model, and `replicas`, which runs one replica of the model per
  GPU: [How many robots can one GPU serve?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-many-robots-can-one-gpu-serve.md)
- **No GPU near the robot.** [How do I get a GPU near my robot?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-get-a-gpu-near-my-robot.md)

## See also

- [Quickstart](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/quickstart.md)
- [FAQ](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/faq.md), for the errors a first run can print
- [Comparison with openpi's and LeRobot's remote inference](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/comparison.md)

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-use-the-inference-components-with-openpi-lerobot-or-gr00t.md

# How do I use the inference components with openpi, LeRobot or GR00T?

Keep the model and the server you have, and add the component that fits where your model spends its time. Which
component applies depends on the framework the policy runs in, not on its name:

| Your policy | `cuda_graphs` | `batcher` and `slack` | `replicas` |
|---|---|---|---|
| A PyTorch policy with a denoising loop: GR00T, LeRobot's diffusion and flow policies, or your own | Applies. Measured on GR00T N1.7 only | Apply where your model takes a batch | One replica per GPU |
| openpi's models under JAX (π0, π0.5) | Does not apply: it is for PyTorch, and π0.5 under JAX was already 98% GPU-busy | Apply. Measured on π0.5's batched call, and `slack` in a test server around it | One replica per GPU. Measured: two on one GPU gained nothing |

What follows is where each component goes and what was measured on the models themselves.

## GR00T, and other PyTorch policies: a faster forward pass

```python
from sequence_ai.engine import cuda_graphs

census = cuda_graphs.Census(cuda_graphs.modules_of(policy))
for _ in range(3):
    policy_answer = run_policy(policy, observation)      # one inference, as your code makes it
    census.end_act()
census.close()
paths = [row["path"] for row in census.candidates()]    # the module called many times per run comes first
cuda_graphs.install(policy, paths[:1])                   # from here on, replayed and checked byte for byte
```

Measured: GR00T N1.7 on an L4, its DiT captured, 224 ms to 146 ms per run, with exactly the same outputs on inputs it
was not captured on. The census shows in three runs whether your model has a module worth graphing, and
[`examples/check_on_a_gpu.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/check_on_a_gpu.py) shows how to compare every output with eager mode's on
your GPU.
[How do I make a PyTorch robot policy faster without changing its outputs?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-make-a-pytorch-robot-policy-faster-without-changing-its-outputs.md)

## openpi and LeRobot: more than one robot on a GPU

openpi's policy server calls the model once for each request, with no batching across connections, and LeRobot 0.7's
policy server holds one robot session (both verified in their source code:
[the comparison page](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/comparison.md)). To
serve several robots in one forward pass, the requests must reach the model as a batch, which requires your own
handler around the model's batched call:

```python
from sequence_ai.engine.batcher import Batcher

batcher = Batcher(infer_a_batch, sizes=[1, 2, 4], wait_ms=2.0)    # infer_a_batch(observations: list) -> list
output = await batcher(observation)                                # in each connection's handler
```

You write `infer_a_batch`: it stacks the observations, calls the model once, and splits the output. For an openpi
policy that is each observation through the policy's input transform, the results stacked, one call of the model's
`sample_actions`, and each row through the output transform. Measured on π0.5 on an L4 with the model's own batched
call: 5.99 requests per second at batch 1 and 10.66 at batch 16. That model's time is mostly in its prefix, which
batching does not amortize, so the gain levels off near 1.78 times. Through the transforms, batches of 1, 2, 4 and 8
took 195, 312, 540 and 1,027 ms, 1.52 times at batch 8, and each size compiled for 32 to 43 s on its first call.

A server that holds a batch by each robot's slack runs its own loop with `slack` in place of `Batcher`. That loop was
run around π0.5's batched call with openpi's own client: the capacity `slack` computed, 2 robots on one L4 for a
15 Hz policy, had no late response, and 3 robots had 21 to 26%. Batching added no capacity on that model and GPU:
openpi's own server, one request at a time, served the same 2 robots. For SmolVLA the formula `slack` then used for
the load gave too high a capacity, and the capacity is computed on a clock since:
[Why the capacity is computed on a clock](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-many-robots-can-one-gpu-serve.md#why-the-capacity-is-computed-on-a-clock).
[How many robots can one GPU serve?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-many-robots-can-one-gpu-serve.md#checked-on-a-real-model)

## Any of them: the model off the server's event loop

```python
from sequence_ai.engine.replicas import ReplicaPool

pool = ReplicaPool(load, replicas=1)                     # load() builds the policy in its own process
output = await pool.run(observation)
```

One replica per GPU. With π0.5 on an L4, two replicas on one GPU each took 2.1 times as long.
[Should I run two replicas of a policy on one GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/should-i-run-two-replicas-of-a-policy-on-one-gpu.md)

## The connection to the robot

The inference components run on the server. For the link between the robot and the GPU, with openpi's own client or
LeRobot's remote inference kept as they are, the network layer adds one line on openpi's client
([How do I run π0 (openpi) on a remote GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-run-pi0-openpi-on-a-remote-gpu.md)) or one Zenoh setting for
LeRobot
([How do I reduce the latency of LeRobot remote inference?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-reduce-the-latency-of-lerobot-remote-inference.md)).

## Limitations

- No inference component has been run inside openpi's own policy server or LeRobot's. `slack` was run once around
  π0.5's batched call, in a test server that speaks openpi's protocol to openpi's own client.
- `cuda_graphs` has been measured on GR00T N1.7 only. LeRobot's policies and openpi's PyTorch models have not been
  tested with it, and it does not apply to models under JAX.
- Two replicas on one GPU gained nothing with π0.5 on an L4.

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-many-robots-can-one-gpu-serve.md

# How many robots can one GPU serve?

As many as can be answered within the buffer their action chunks leave. A policy that responds with a chunk of
actions leaves its robot some steps still to execute when it requests the next chunk: that buffer, less the robot's
round-trip time (RTT) and a margin, is how long a batch may take. `slack.Seating` turns a timing table and three
policy parameters into a capacity, and names the robots a replica of the model cannot serve. `batcher` then sends
their requests as batches.

```python
from sequence_ai.engine import slack

table = slack.measure(forward_of, sizes=[1, 2, 4])               # forward_of(n): one forward pass of n requests
play = slack.playback(hz=20, valid_len=15, replan_at=8)          # 15 valid steps, the next requested at the 8th
seating = slack.Seating(table, play["buffer_s"] * 1000, sizes=[1, 2, 4],
                        cycle_ms=(play["play_s"] - play["buffer_s"]) * 1000)
seats, over = seating.seat([("near", 30.0), ("far", 200.0)])     # (robot, its RTT in ms)
```

With batches of 1, 2 and 4 that take 80, 110 and 130 ms, this gives `(4, ["far"])`: the replica has capacity for
four robots, and the one 200 ms away is the one to move to another replica. `python examples/components/slack.py`
prints that case with no model and no GPU.

## The limits

- **Latency.** A robot fits the largest listed batch size whose batch time, plus the robot's own RTT and 50 ms, is
  within the buffer. A robot further away has less of its buffer left for the server, so it fits a smaller batch.
- **The batches a request arrives behind.** A replica runs one batch at a time, and robots send on their own clocks:
  a request that arrives as another batch runs waits for it, and is in time or not depending on how far apart the
  robots' requests fall. No formula has that, so `slack` runs 2, 3 and more robots on a simulated clock, as its
  server loop would serve them, from starts spread evenly over every way their requests can fall in a cycle (64 for
  two robots, 128 for more). A number of robots is within capacity when at least 95% of their responses are back
  before their robot's buffer runs out, each start counting the same.
- **Load.** In each of those starts the robots' batches may fill at most 0.9 of a cycle, the time between one robot's
  requests. Past that, responses queue behind each other however the requests are batched.

The first number of robots that fails ends the count: robots are admitted one at a time, so a replica reaches a
number of robots through every smaller one. In the example above a batch of four fits the buffer of a robot 100 ms
away (130 + 100 + 50 ms, within 350), and the capacity is four: on the clock four such robots have every response in
time, and their batches fill no more than 0.68 of a cycle.

Each robot is evaluated by its own RTT. When every robot was evaluated by the furthest robot's RTT, one far robot
lowered the batch size, and with it the capacity, of every near robot on the same replica.

## What batching itself gains

It depends on where the model spends its time. Measured on π0.5 on an L4, with the model's own batched call:

| Batch size | 1 | 2 | 4 | 8 | 16 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Requests per second | 5.99 | 8.21 | 9.38 | 10.52 | 10.66 |

That is 1.78 times at batch 16, and most of it by batch 4. That model spends most of a call on its prefix, the
images and the prompt, and batching does not amortize the prefix: 138 ms per request at batch 1, 119 ms at batch 16.
What batching does amortize is the action head, from about 53 ms to about 2 ms per request. **A model that spends
most of its time in the prefix gains correspondingly little.** These numbers are the model's, not `batcher`'s, which
has unit tests and no measurement of its own.

A server does not reach the model's batched call directly: each observation goes through the policy's input transform
first, and each row of the output through its output transform. Timed that way, also with π0.5 on an L4, batches of 1,
2, 3, 4 and 8 took 195, 312, 429, 540 and 1,027 ms: 5.1 requests per second at batch 1 and 7.8 at batch 8, 1.52 times.
Under JAX each batch size compiled on its first call, in 32 to 43 s.

## Sending the batches

```python
from sequence_ai.engine.batcher import Batcher

batcher = Batcher(model_on_a_list, sizes=[1, 2, 4, 8], wait_ms=2.0)    # model_on_a_list(inputs: list) -> list
output = await batcher(observation)                                     # in each request's handler
```

- A batch is dispatched as soon as it is full, or `wait_ms` after its first call arrived while the model is free.
- While the model is busy, waiting calls keep accumulating and are dispatched together as soon as it is free.
- Only the sizes you list are sent: with sizes `[1, 2, 4]`, three waiting calls are dispatched as a batch of 2, then
  a batch of 1.
- A batch in which the model raised is re-run call by call, so only the call that fails by itself fails.

`Batcher` waits one fixed time for every caller and has no notion of a robot. A server that holds a batch by each
robot's slack asks `slack.Aligner` how long the open batch may wait and which requests are dispatched first:
[`docs/slack.md`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/slack.md) has the rules and a loop.

## Checked on a real model

One run checked whether the capacity `slack` computed was the capacity a real model has. For this model it was, and
on this model and GPU batching added no capacity: openpi's own server, one request at a time, served the same robots
in time. `slack` then computed the load by a formula, which gave too high a capacity for a model with slower batches:
[Why the capacity is computed on a clock](#why-the-capacity-is-computed-on-a-clock).

openpi's π0.5 (`pi05_droid`) on one L4, in a test server of about 200 lines that speaks openpi's WebSocket protocol and
runs [the loop in `docs/slack.md`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/slack.md#in-a-server) around the batched call above, with openpi's own client on
each robot. The robots were simulated on the server's machine: each sent a 301 KB observation at the 8th of a
chunk's 15 valid steps, and a relay added an RTT of 20, 50 or 100 ms. A response is late when it arrives after the
buffer has run out. One run per cell, of 60 s, and of 120 s for 4 robots at 20 Hz.

| Policy rate | Buffer | Capacity computed | Robots connected | Late responses |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 15 Hz | 467 ms | 2 | 1 | 0 of 112, at each RTT |
| | | | 2 | 0 of 225, at each RTT |
| | | | 3 | 21.0% and 25.7%, at 20 and 50 ms |
| | | | 4 | 99.2 to 99.7% |
| | | | 8 | 99.5 to 99.8% |
| 20 Hz | 350 ms | 1 | 2 | 39.8% and 89.5%, at 20 and 50 ms |
| | | | 4 | 99.9% |

`slack.per_replica` computed each capacity from the timing table, before any robot connected. At 15 Hz it held: no
response was late with 2 robots, and 21 to 26% were with one more. At 20 Hz one robot was not run, and two, one more
than the capacity, had 40% and 90% of their responses late. The test server admitted every robot that connected:
`Seating.seat()` is what limits a replica to its capacity, and this server did not call it.

Computed on a clock, as it is now, the capacity for these batch times is the same at each RTT. Two robots 100 ms
away are in time unless their requests fall 5 to 25 ms apart, where the second arrives too late to share the first
one's batch and its response, behind that batch, is back after the buffer ran out: 3.9% of their responses over the
starts, within the 5% the rule allows. The cell run with two robots at 100 ms had no late response.

Batching added no capacity here. openpi's own policy server, which runs one request at a time, also served 2 robots
with no late response, and a third would need 586 ms of forward passes in each 533 ms. A batch of 2 takes 312 ms where
two requests one by one take 390 ms, and a batch of 3 takes 429 ms, which with a robot's RTT and the 50 ms margin is
past the 467 ms buffer. Whether batching adds capacity depends on how a model's forward pass grows with its batch
size on a given GPU: [What batching itself gains](#what-batching-itself-gains).

- **At or below the capacity the loop costs nothing.** With 1 and 2 robots the median latency was within 1 ms of
  openpi's own policy server at every RTT, 216 to 304 ms.
- **Above it, batching completes more requests and does not make them arrive in time.** openpi's own server runs one
  request at a time: with 4 and 8 robots it completed 300 to 305 requests in 60 s, at a median latency of 800 to 807 ms
  and 1,615 to 1,627 ms, and 99% of responses were late. The test server completed 360 to 368 and 415 to 419, at 653
  to 667 ms and 1,160 to 1,173 ms, and 99% were late as well.
- **Above it, however a batch waits, responses do not arrive in time.** At 20 Hz two robots need two forward passes,
  about 201 ms each under load, in the 400 ms between a robot's requests, and no batch of two formed. Each run was in
  time until a queue built up, and 85 to 97% late from then on. That took 33.5 s and 4.7 s with `hold_s` (RTTs of 20
  and 50 ms), 7.1 s and 4.3 s with a fixed wait of 2 ms in its place, and 3.9 s and 0.3 s with one of 50 ms. The late
  share of a 60 s run, 39.8 to 89.5%, therefore measures when the queue formed, in one run per cell, and says nothing
  about the waiting rule.

Not measured: openpi's server with 3 robots or at 20 Hz, the test server with one robot at 20 Hz, and anything of
the network layer, because the relay adds delay only, with no loss and no idle restart. One GPU, one model and one
run per cell.

## Why the capacity is computed on a clock

The same check with three models, each on one L4 with simulated robots of a 15 Hz policy (a 467 ms buffer, a request
every 533 ms) 20 ms away, 60 s per cell, and two draws of when each robot starts. `slack` then computed the load by a
formula:

| Model | A batch of 1, 2, 4, 8 | Capacity by the formula | Measured | Capacity on a clock |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| π0.5 | 198, 320, 565 ms (no 8) | 2 | 2 robots: no late response in 4 cells | 2 |
| GR00T N1.6 | 223, 273, 399 ms (no 8) | 2 | 2 robots: no late response in 3 cells, 0.4% late in a fourth | 2 |
| SmolVLA | 256, 273, 303, 377 ms | 8 | 4 robots: 95.4% and 96.8% late. 8 robots: 99.2% and 99.6% late | 1 |

The formula assumed that robots whose batches of one size do not fit in a cycle share larger batches: four SmolVLA
robots as one batch of four, 303 ms of each 533. They did not. Robots send on their own clocks, and nothing brings
their requests together. The four ran as two fixed pairs in turn, each request behind the other pair's batch: 273 ms,
273 ms and the RTT, a median of 553 ms against a buffer of 467. A round of two pairs takes 546 ms, more than the
533 ms between a robot's requests, so after the first 4 to 6 s every response was late. The formula also returned the
largest number of robots that passed it, and with these times two failed where three to eight passed.

`slack` now runs the robots on a clock, which has both. [`examples/fleet_on_a_clock.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/fleet_on_a_clock.py)
prints what it runs, here with SmolVLA's times:

```bash
python examples/fleet_on_a_clock.py --times 1:256,2:273,4:303,8:377
```

```text
  robots   responses in time   starts with a late response   load
       1             100.0%                0 of 1             0.48
       2             100.0%                0 of 64            0.53 to 0.96
       3              51.5%              125 of 128           1.00 to 1.01
       4               0.8%              127 of 128           0.57 to 1.05
       5               0.0%              128 of 128           1.04 to 1.31
       6               0.0%              128 of 128           1.09
       7               0.0%              128 of 128           1.28
       8               3.7%              128 of 128           1.05 to 1.14

slack.per_replica computes a capacity of 1 for these times (8 by the buffer alone): the first number of robots
with fewer than 95% of its responses in time over the starts, or a load above 0.9 in one of them, ends the count.
```

Four robots have nearly every response late, as on the L4. Two are in time in every start, at a load of 0.53 where
their requests fall close enough to share a batch and 0.96 where they do not. 0.96 is above the 0.9 limit, so the
capacity is 1. That limit was set on one stand-in model ([below](#what-the-load-limit-was-measured-on)).

It is a clock, not a model: every batch takes its timed p95, rounded up by 3% at most, nothing else runs beside it,
and the starts are a sample. Rerun on the model, SmolVLA on an L4 with simulated robots about 30 ms away, it gave a
capacity of 1 again, and the robots did this:

| Robots connected | Their requests | Run | Late responses |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 150 ms apart | 60 s | 0 of 226 |
| 2 | 270 ms apart | 300 s | 0 of 1,125 |
| 3 | together | 60 s | 18 of 339 (5.3%), all in the first 5.4 s |
| 3 | evenly spread | 60 s | 97 of 338 (28.7%) |
| 3, and the server asked `Seating.seat()` as each connected | drawn from a seed | 30 s | one admitted, 0 of 57 late; two refused |

Three robots were late, as on the clock. Two were not, in either run: the clock has them in time as well, and
refuses the second for its load. The 0.9 is kept: at 0.96 of a cycle little is left for a network or a GPU that
varies, and these robots ran on the server's own machine. One run per cell.

## What the load limit was measured on

Four robots, 300 s and about 2,100 requests per run, on a stand-in model on a CPU paced like a 15 Hz policy (15 valid
steps, the next requested at the 8th: a 467 ms buffer, 533 ms between a robot's requests; batches of 1, 2 and 4 in
234, 254 and 299 ms). All four on one replica, a load of 0.95, had 85.7% of their responses back within the 467 ms.
Two per replica on two replicas, a load of 0.88, had 94.1%, on the slower network of the two runs. The 0.9 is set from
those two runs, in the serving stack `slack` was taken from, not with the file itself.

## Limitations

- **A policy that leaves no slack.** Where the robot sends a request only when a chunk is fully executed, a replica
  serves one robot.
- **A robot that does not report its RTT** is assumed to have 100 ms. If it is further away, its responses arrive
  late.
- **A model whose time depends on its input** is timed by the p95 of its batch size alone.
- **The capacity comes from a simulated clock**, not from your model under load:
  [what the clock leaves out](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/slack.md#limitations).
- **More replicas on the same GPU do not add capacity:**
  [Should I run two replicas of a policy on one GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/should-i-run-two-replicas-of-a-policy-on-one-gpu.md)

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md

# What do the components save, measured with the tools in this repository?

On a clean link between two cloud machines, an upload that follows a robot's half-second pause took two to three round
trips with the defaults, and one with any of the components that keep the connection from going idle. That held over
plain TCP, over a WebSocket and over Zenoh, at round-trip times (RTTs) from 11 to 101 ms. At 242 ms the pause cost
nothing, and under 1% packet loss a ping did not help where BBR did.

Everything on this page was measured on 2026-11-15 with [`bench/`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/tree/main/bench), as released. It is one pair of machines
on one night. **It is not a promise for your link:**
[measure yours](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-measure-the-link-between-my-robot-and-my-gpu.md).

## The setup

- **Two machines** of one cloud provider, in two regions 11 to 12 ms apart by `ping`, each with 2 shared vCPUs and
  2 GB of memory. Ubuntu 24.04, Linux 7.0, CUBIC as the default congestion control, and
  `net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle=1`, the kernel's default.
- **One is the server and one the client.** There is no GPU and no model: the far end responds with a few bytes, so
  every millisecond below is the transport's.
- **Longer RTTs are the same link with delay added** where the robot's packets leave
  (`tc qdisc add dev IF root netem delay Nms`).
- **No run inherits another's window:** `net.ipv4.tcp_no_metrics_save=1`, and `ip tcp_metrics flush all` before
  each run.
- **A cell is 40 uploads** after 3 that are not counted (20 in the table of sizes). An upload "took more than one
  round trip" when it took over 1.5 times its run's baseline: the median of small requests on the warm connection.
- **The pause is counted from the response.** After the response to one upload arrives, the client waits (0.53 s,
  or 0.5 s in the table of sizes) and uploads again. The connection has then sent nothing for the pause plus one
  RTT.

## An upload after a pause, over TCP

A 24 KB upload 0.53 s after each response, on a connection first widened with one 1 MB upload
(`bench/client.py --sizes 24k --idle-ms 530 --samples 40 --warm 1m`). Each cell is the median upload in round trips,
and how many of the 40 took more than one.

| RTT | Default | The server pings every 100 ms | The client sends a byte every 100 ms | BBR on the robot's socket | `tcp_slow_start_after_idle=0` on the robot |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 12.4 ms | **1.99 (40 of 40)** | 1.01 (0) | 1.01 (0) | 1.01 (0) | 1.01 (0) |
| 21.4 ms | **2.00 (40 of 40)** | 1.01 (0) | 1.01 (0) | 1.00 (0) | 1.01 (0) |
| 40.5 ms | **1.99 (40 of 40)** | 1.00 (0) | 1.00 (0) | 1.00 (0) | 1.00 (0) |
| 65.5 ms | **2.00 (40 of 40)** | 1.00 (0) | 1.00 (0) | 1.01 (0) | 1.00 (0) |
| 81.3 ms | **2.00 (40 of 40)** | 1.00 (0) | 1.00 (0) | 1.00 (0) | 1.00 (0) |
| 100.7 ms | **2.00 (40 of 40)** | 1.00 (0) | 1.00 (0) | 1.00 (0) | 1.00 (0) |
| 242.2 ms | 1.00 (0 of 40) | 1.00 (0) | 1.00 (0) | 1.01 (0) | 1.00 (0) |

In milliseconds, the default against the server's ping: 24.7 against 12.5, 42.7 against 21.5, 80.6 against 40.4,
130.6 against 65.5, 162.3 against 81.4, 201.3 against 100.9, and 242.4 against 242.3.

**Why 242 ms took no extra round trip.** The kernel halves an idle connection's window once for each retransmission
timeout that passed, and the timeout is about the RTT plus 200 ms. Up to 101 ms, the pause plus one RTT spanned two
timeouts: the window, 28 packets before each upload, was cut to 10, the least it is cut to, and the upload left in two
flights. At 242 ms they spanned one: the window, 36 packets before each upload, became 18, and the whole upload left at
once.

**Why this differs from an earlier measurement at about 101 ms.** With a robot that uploaded on a fixed period of
0.53 s, counted from the start of one upload to the start of the next, the same 24 KB upload took no extra round trip
at about 101 ms: that silence spans one timeout, not two. Here the 0.53 s is counted from the response, which matches
a robot that starts its pause when the response arrives. **At about 100 ms the two ways of counting the same half
second fall on either side of the edge.** A robot's pause, its RTT and its upload's size decide together, and a small
change in any of them can move a link across.

## Larger uploads

Uploads 0.5 s after each response, with no widening first
(`bench/client.py --sizes 100k,500k,1m --idle-ms 500 --samples 20 --modes idle,ping,keepwarm,continuous`). Median in
round trips; in brackets, how many of the 20 took more than one.

| RTT | Upload | Default | The server pings | The client sends | One after another, no pause |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 13.2 ms | 100 KB | **2.98 (20)** | 1.10 (0) | 1.08 (0) | 1.06 (0) |
| 13.2 ms | 500 KB | **2.99 (20)** | 1.23 (1) | 1.24 (0) | 1.15 (0) |
| 13.2 ms | 1 MB | **3.01 (20)** | 1.31 (1) | 1.36 (0) | 1.35 (8) |
| 81.3 ms | 100 KB | **2.99 (20)** | 1.00 (0) | 1.00 (0) | 1.00 (0) |
| 81.3 ms | 500 KB | **3.00 (20)** | 1.01 (0) | 1.01 (0) | 1.01 (0) |
| 81.3 ms | 1 MB | **2.01 (20)** | 1.02 (0) | 1.01 (0) | 1.01 (0) |

At 13 ms, 1 MB takes over one round trip even with no pause at all: at that distance the time to push a megabyte
through is no longer small beside the RTT. That is the link's rate, and none of these components changes it.

## A camera stream

Frames at a fixed rate with no pause longer than the frame period
(`bench/client.py --modes stream --stream 30x50k,10x100k --seconds 10`), at the 12 ms RTT: 50 KB frames at
30 Hz took a median of 1.02 round trips each, none of 300 over one; 100 KB frames at 10 Hz took 1.09, none of 100.
**A robot that streams has no pause that costs a round trip, and nothing here to gain.**

## With 1% packet loss

The 24 KB upload again, with `netem` dropping 1% of the robot's packets.

| RTT | CUBIC, default | CUBIC, the client sends through the pause | BBR on the robot's socket |
|---|---|---|---|
| 22 ms | **2.00 (40 of 40)** | **2.00 (31 of 40)** | 1.01 (0 of 40) |
| 101.5 ms | **2.00 (40 of 40)** | **2.00 (35 of 40)** | not measured |

**Under loss the ping did not help.** The window before each upload was a median of 14 packets, fewer than the upload
needs: the losses had cut it, not the pause, and a ping keeps a window from being restarted but does not grow one. BBR
does not set its window by losses, and took no extra round trip at 22 ms. BBR at 101.5 ms with loss was not measured.

## Over a WebSocket, and over Zenoh

A 100 KB upload 0.53 s after each response, 40 per cell, on a connection first widened with one 1 MB upload
([`bench/ws_bench.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/bench/ws_bench.py), [`bench/zenoh_bench.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/bench/zenoh_bench.py)). Each cell is the
median in milliseconds and, in brackets, in round trips. Without a component, 40 of 40 uploads took more than one round
trip in every row; with one, none did.

| RTT | WebSocket, as it is | The server pings ([`ping`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/ping.py)) | The client keeps it warm ([`openpi.keep`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/openpi.py)) | BBR alone on the robot's socket | Zenoh, as it is | Zenoh with the keep-alive file ([`lerobot`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/lerobot.py)) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 11.3 ms | **37.6 (3.3)** | 13.4 (1.2) | 12.7 (1.1) | 12.7 (1.1) | **38.1 (3.4)** | 13.9 (1.2) |
| 21.4 ms | **44.4 (2.1)** | 23.5 (1.1) | 22.7 (1.1) | 23.7 (1.1) | **44.8 (2.1)** | 23.2 (1.1) |
| 40.5 ms | **82.4 (2.0)** | 41.8 (1.0) | 41.8 (1.0) | 43.7 (1.1) | **82.8 (2.0)** | 42.3 (1.0) |
| 80.5 ms | **163.8 (2.0)** | 82.8 (1.0) | 82.6 (1.0) | 87.1 (1.1) | **164.3 (2.0)** | 82.2 (1.0) |

What these two columns are:

- **The WebSocket rows use the `websockets` library on both ends**, the library openpi's server and client are built on,
  with compression off as openpi has it. `openpi.keep()` ran on a stand-in for openpi's client: an object with the two
  members `keep()` uses, the connection and `infer`. Not tested with openpi's own policy server and client, or with a
  model. In the `openpi.keep` column the machine had no BBR to give, so what kept the window was the ping.
- **The Zenoh rows are two Zenoh peers**, one answering the other's requests, with and without the file
  `lerobot.keep_alive_file()` writes, given to both. Not tested with LeRobot's own policy server and robot.

## `openpi.keep()` with openpi's own server and client

One closed-loop run with openpi's own policy server (the `pi05_droid` checkpoint, on an L4) and openpi's own client,
with and without `kept = openpi.keep(policy)`. The client ran in a Linux virtual machine (kernel 6.8, default settings,
CUBIC) on a laptop on a home connection; its kernel measured a smoothed RTT of 38 to 66 ms and a retransmission timeout
of about 240 to 270 ms. Each request uploaded 301 KB, and each row is one 45 s episode. "Outside inference" is the time
`policy.infer()` took on the client minus the inference time the server reported (about 195 ms).

| Setting | Outside inference, p50 (p95) | Idle before a request, p50 | Uploads during which the window fell to about half | Retransmissions |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| As it is | **181.4** (237.1) ms | 346 ms | 86 of 89 | 25 |
| As it is | **151.9** (223.5) ms | 378 ms | 85 of 89 | 58 |
| `openpi.keep()` | 92.1 (132.9) ms | 65 ms | 0 of 89 | 0 |
| `openpi.keep()` | 156.7 (334.8) ms | 90 ms | 4 of 87 | 48 |
| `openpi.keep()`, BBR module loaded | 85.6 (109.8) ms | 80 ms | 3 of 90 | 9 |
| `openpi.keep()`, BBR module loaded | 90.6 (136.3) ms | 78 ms | 2 of 90 | 25 |

Without `keep()` the connection was idle for longer than its retransmission timeout before almost every request, and
the kernel reduced the congestion window before the upload. With `keep()` the idle time just before each request was
under 100 ms, and the window fell during 0 to 4 uploads in an episode. Neither measure sees a cut made earlier, at the
robot's first ping after the answer: openpi's server answers no ping while it runs inference, so the robot's ping waits,
and the robot can go longer than a retransmission timeout without sending (below). The second `keep()` episode lost
packets (48 retransmissions) and its median was no better
than without `keep()`: a ping does not help against loss. With the BBR module loaded (`sudo modprobe tcp_bbr`, after
which `kept.bbr` is true) both episodes matched the loss-free `keep()` episode.

This is one link and two episodes per setting, and the client was a virtual machine whose packets the laptop forwards,
not a robot's own Linux computer.

A later run counted where the window is cut. Two Linux cloud machines ran openpi's own client (CUBIC, no BBR), 30 and
75 ms from openpi's own server (the `pi05_droid` checkpoint, on an L4), each six 45 s episodes with and without
`keep()`, 301 KB per request. "Halved before the request" counts the requests whose window just before the request was
half the window after the previous upload: Linux cut it at a send in between, the robot's first ping after a silence
longer than its retransmission timeout.

| Robot | `keep()` | Halved before the request | Window left, p50 (packets) | Outside inference, p50 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 30 ms away | no | 3 of 429 | 72 | 91.2 ms |
| 30 ms away | yes | 373 of 482 | 215 | 37.1 ms |
| 75 ms away | no | 3 of 477 | 215 | 86.7 ms |
| 75 ms away | yes | 270 of 477 | 216 | 100.5 ms |

Without `keep()` the window was cut at the request itself, twice at 30 ms (286 to 72 packets). With `keep()` it was cut
once, earlier, and the 301 KB upload (209 packets) still fitted in the 215 left in most requests (79% at 30 ms, all at
75 ms); a larger one would not have. BBR on the robot avoids the restart
([`window.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/window.py)).

## Pictures as JPEG with openpi's own server and client

One closed-loop run with openpi's own policy server (the `pi05_droid` checkpoint, on an L4) and openpi's own client,
the robot a simulated arm on a Mac on a home connection, two pictures of 224 x 224 in each request: first as arrays, as
openpi's guide sends them, then as JPEG, each fitted and encoded as `openpi.image_tools` does it, with the server
pinging each connection every 100 ms and decoding the pictures as `openpi.patch()` makes it do. Each row is one 45 s
episode on the same GPU. "Outside the server" is the round trip the client measured minus the inference time the
server reported; the RTT is a TCP echo to the GPU, measured during the episode.

| Pictures | Upload per request | Outside the server, p50 (p95) | RTT, p50 | Frame to answer, p50 (p95) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Arrays | 301.5 KB | 153.8 (270.8) ms | 56.5 ms | 351.8 (468.0) ms |
| JPEG, the server pinging | 18.8 KB | **58.1** (207.8) ms | 37.5 ms | 279.6 (429.6) ms |

The link was faster during the second episode, so take its RTT out: the time outside the server beyond one RTT fell
from about 97 ms to about 21 ms. The server took longer for each inference in the second episode, 219.7 against
195.0 ms at the median, while the model's own time was the same (149.8 and 149.3 ms). That server was started through
another script, as `python -m sequence_ai.network.openpi` starts it, and it was as slow with the pings and the decoding
taken out: the difference is in how it was started, and its cause is not known.

This is one link and one episode per setting, and the pings and the JPEG were not measured apart.

## From a Linux client on a home connection

An upload over a WebSocket 0.5 s after the previous response, 16 per cell: the median in milliseconds and, in brackets,
in round trips of that row. The client was the same Linux virtual machine (kernel 6.8, default settings, CUBIC) on a
laptop on a home connection, or the laptop itself (macOS). The server used the `websockets` library, and in the ping
rows it pinged with `ping_interval=0.1`, which is what `ping.websockets_options()` sets.

| Client | RTT | 100 KB | 500 KB | 1 MB |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Linux, as it is | 34.9 ms | **192.5 (5.5)** | 359.7 (10.3) | 467.0 (13.4) |
| Linux, the server pings every 0.1 s | 35.0 ms | 59.8 (1.7) | 271.6 (7.8) | 445.2 (12.7) |
| Linux, `tcp_slow_start_after_idle=0` | 29.1 ms | 57.7 (2.0) | 392.1 (13.5) | 465.4 (16.0) |
| Linux, BBR on the client's socket | 30.6 ms | 60.0 (2.0) | 157.4 (5.1) | 255.5 (8.3) |
| macOS, as it is | 34.2 ms | 89.4 (2.6) | 135.9 (4.0) | 229.2 (6.7) |
| macOS, the server pings every 0.1 s | 33.1 ms | 89.5 (2.7) | 121.0 (3.7) | 247.2 (7.5) |

At 100 KB the idle restart is the cost: with default settings the window was at 38 segments after 547 ms of idle time,
and the ping, the kernel option and BBR each brought the upload to about two round trips. At 500 KB and 1 MB the line's
upload rate and its packet loss were the cost: six 500 KB uploads sent back to back with default settings took a median
of 14.9 round trips, more than after a pause. There the ping and the kernel option changed little, and BBR took 5.1 and
8.3 round trips where the default settings took 10.3 and 13.4. macOS keeps its window through a pause, and the ping
made no consistent difference there.

This is one home line, a virtual machine and 16 uploads per cell.

## Limitations

- **One clean link for the tables above the last two.** A datacenter network between two machines: no Wi-Fi, no home
  line, no cellular hop, and loss only as `netem`'s random 1%. The two sections above this one are from one home
  connection. On the same kind of connection with a cellular uplink, an earlier measurement found the server's ping
  gave no benefit that six uploads could show: [the README's limitations](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/README.md#limitations).
- **No model.** A real policy takes hundreds of milliseconds to respond. A round trip saved is the same number of
  milliseconds either way, and a smaller share of the whole.
- **One pause.** 0.53 s after the response (0.5 s for the sizes). A robot that sends its next request sooner than its
  RTT plus 200 ms never takes the extra round trip; one that pauses for seconds has its window cut to its floor.
- **One upload size for the first table.** At about 100 ms a 24 KB upload is at the boundary described above, and a
  smaller or larger one may fall on the other side of it.
- **The last hop can matter more than the distance.** On the home connection, a laptop that scanned for Wi-Fi
  networks every 20 seconds raised a 30 Hz stream of 50 KB frames from a median of 43 ms per frame to 181 ms.

## Repeat it

On the server side:

```bash
python3 bench/server.py --port 9000
python3 bench/ws_bench.py server 9101 & python3 bench/ws_bench.py server 9102 --ping
python3 bench/zenoh_bench.py server 7447 & python3 bench/zenoh_bench.py server 7448 --keep
```

On the client side (Linux, as root for the first three lines):

```bash
sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_no_metrics_save=1 && ip tcp_metrics flush all
tc qdisc replace dev IF root netem delay 30ms                 # a longer RTT: the delay to add; `loss 1%` too
modprobe tcp_bbr                                              # lets a socket request BBR; the default stays CUBIC

python3 bench/client.py --host HOST --sizes 24k --idle-ms 530 --samples 40 --modes idle,ping,keepwarm --warm 1m
python3 bench/client.py --host HOST --sizes 24k --idle-ms 530 --samples 40 --modes idle --warm 1m --bbr
python3 bench/client.py --host HOST --sizes 100k,500k,1m --idle-ms 500 --samples 20 \
    --modes idle,ping,keepwarm,continuous
python3 bench/client.py --host HOST --modes stream --stream 30x50k,10x100k --seconds 10

python3 bench/ws_bench.py client HOST 9101 plain              # as it is
python3 bench/ws_bench.py client HOST 9102 plain              # the server pings
python3 bench/ws_bench.py client HOST 9101 keep               # openpi.keep on the client side
python3 bench/ws_bench.py client HOST 9101 bbr                # BBR alone
python3 bench/zenoh_bench.py client HOST 7447                 # as it is
python3 bench/zenoh_bench.py client HOST 7448 --keep          # the keep-alive file on both ends
```

The kernel option's column is the first command again after `sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle=0`.
[`bench/README.md`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/bench/README.md) describes what each block sends.

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/quickstart-inference.md

# Quickstart: from `pip install` to a batched response

Two commands and one short file give you five robots sending requests concurrently, their requests batched, and the
model running in its own process. No GPU, no model and no torch are needed for these steps. The output shown is
from the package built from this repository at 0.62.0, on macOS on Apple silicon with Python 3.12; Python 3.10 or later
behaves the same way.

**How long it takes.** The install took 2 seconds with the packages already downloaded, and the file ran in 0.3 seconds.

## 1. Install

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install sequence-ai
```

The last line it prints:

```text
Successfully installed annotated-types-0.8.0 anyio-4.16.0 certifi-2026.10.23 h11-0.16.0 httpcore-1.0.9 httpx-0.28.1 idna-3.20 pillow-13.0.0 pydantic-2.14.3 pydantic-core-2.50.4 sequence-ai-0.62.0 sequence-base-0.8.12 typing-extensions-4.16.0 typing-inspection-0.4.5
```

The inference components import only the standard library. `cuda_graphs` operates on a torch model, and uses the torch
your model already has.

## 2. Run five robots against one model

Save this as `quickstart_batching.py`. It is [`examples/quickstart_batching.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/quickstart_batching.py).

```python
import asyncio
import os
import time

from sequence_ai.engine.batcher import Batcher
from sequence_ai.engine.replicas import ReplicaPool


def load():
    """Runs in the replica's own process: build your model here, and return what one batch of requests runs."""
    def model_on_a_list(observations: list) -> list:
        time.sleep(0.05)                                   # one forward pass, whatever the batch: your model's call
        return [{"actions": [[observation] * 7] * 8, "pid": os.getpid()} for observation in observations]

    return model_on_a_list


async def main() -> None:
    pool = ReplicaPool(load, replicas=1)                   # one replica per GPU; devices=[0] sets the GPU it sees
    batcher = Batcher(pool.run, sizes=[1, 2, 4, 8], wait_ms=2.0)
    try:
        started = time.perf_counter()
        # in your own server, each request's handler awaits batcher(observation)
        outputs = await asyncio.gather(*(batcher(float(robot)) for robot in range(5)))
        took = (time.perf_counter() - started) * 1e3
        print(f"5 robots served in {took:.0f} ms, as batches of {dict(batcher.sent)}")
        actions = outputs[3]["actions"]
        print(f"robot 3's own response: {len(actions)} actions of {len(actions[0])} numbers, "
              f"the first {actions[0][:3]}")
        print(f"this process is {os.getpid()}; the model ran in {outputs[3]['pid']}")
    finally:
        pool.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

```bash
python quickstart_batching.py
```

It prints (your process IDs will differ):

```text
5 robots served in 113 ms, as batches of {4: 1, 1: 1}
robot 3's own response: 8 actions of 7 numbers, the first [3.0, 3.0, 3.0]
this process is 73513; the model ran in 73515
```

## What just ran

| What | Why | Component |
|---|---|---|
| Five requests went to the model as a batch of 4 and a batch of 1: two forward passes of 50 ms instead of five | Calls waiting for a model are served in one forward pass; only the sizes you list are sent, because a model is traced, compiled or graphed for the shapes it has seen | [`batcher`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/engine/batcher.py) |
| Robot 3 received its own response, not its batch's | A batch's outputs are split back per call | [`batcher`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/engine/batcher.py) |
| The model ran in another process | A forward pass never blocks your server's event loop, and a replica that dies is replaced | [`replicas`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/engine/replicas.py) |

**The 113 ms is the stand-in model's.** Its forward pass sleeps 50 ms regardless of batch size. What batching gains on
a real model depends on where the model spends its time:
[How many robots can one GPU serve?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-many-robots-can-one-gpu-serve.md)

## Use your own model

1. **Your model.** In `load`, build your model and return a function that takes a list of observations and returns a
   list of outputs, one per observation. `load` is defined at the top of a module, because each replica imports it in
   its own process.
2. **Your server.** In each request's handler, `output = await batcher(observation)`. Any async server works; the
   components are independent of HTTP.
3. **Your GPU.** `ReplicaPool(load, replicas=2, devices=[0, 1])` gives each replica its own GPU. On one GPU use one
   replica: [Should I run two replicas of a policy on one GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/should-i-run-two-replicas-of-a-policy-on-one-gpu.md)
4. **Your batch sizes.** List the sizes your model has been run with, and always include 1.

## Then: a faster forward pass, with the same outputs

If your model is a PyTorch model that calls one module many times per run (a diffusion or flow policy's denoiser),
one more call replays that module from CUDA graphs. With torch installed:

```bash
python examples/graph_a_module.py
```

On a machine with no CUDA GPU it finds the module, leaves the model unchanged, and prints:

```text
candidates: [{'path': 'denoiser', 'calls': 10, 'ms': 1.05}]
cuda graphs: no CUDA GPU available: nothing captured
same outputs, byte for byte: True
eager 1.14 ms per run; no CUDA GPU available, so nothing was graphed
```

On a GPU it captures the module, checks the output against eager mode's byte for byte, and prints both timings.
[How do I make a PyTorch robot policy faster without changing its outputs?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-make-a-pytorch-robot-policy-faster-without-changing-its-outputs.md)

## Where to go next

- [How do I use the inference components with openpi, LeRobot or GR00T?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-use-the-inference-components-with-openpi-lerobot-or-gr00t.md)

- A step failed: [FAQ](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/faq.md)
